1. Flight of peasants
2. Peasant revolts such as those of the Jats, Satnamis and Marathas
3. Expansion of profitable jagir land
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
133.x: Irfan Habib linked over-exploitation by jagirdars with peasant flight and revolts, including those of the Jats, Satnamis and Marathas. It did not expand profitable jagir land.
133.tq: Separate the stated consequences from an opposite effect inserted as a trap.

133.s:
Arrange the following developments in the most appropriate sequence of explanation of the jagirdari crisis:
A. Increase in the number of mansabdars
B. Shrinkage of profitable paibaqi land
C. Greater pressure on peasants
D. Agrarian ruin and decline
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
133.x: The growth of mansabdars coincided with the reduction of profitable land, encouraging harsher extraction from peasants and contributing to agrarian ruin and decline.
133.tq: Follow the causal chain from structural pressure to social consequence.

133.s: Why were Mughal jagirs frequently transferred, generally after about three to four years?
o: To convert all jagirs into Khalisa lands
To make them hereditary among local chiefs
To prevent mansabdars from developing local roots and becoming independent feudal lords
To ensure that peasants elected their revenue collectors
133.x: Frequent transfers, usually every three to four years, were intended to prevent mansabdars from establishing local bases and becoming independent feudal lords.
133.tq: Link the numerical interval with the administrative purpose rather than treating it as an isolated figure.
133.sec: Transfer of jagirs and bejagiri - effects on nobility

133.s:
Consider the following statements about the effects of frequent jagir transfers:
1. Short-term jagirdars had little stake in the long-term prosperity of peasants.
2. They could squeeze peasants to maximise immediate extraction.
3. Frequent transfers eliminated factionalism at the Mughal court.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
133.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Frequent transfers contributed to short-term extraction; they did not eliminate factionalism at court.
133.tq: Reject the absolute or reversed effect in the third statement.
133.sec: Transfer of jagirs and bejagiri - effects on nobility

133.s: The term ‘bejagiri’ refers to a situation in which:
o: Mansabdars were kept waiting without jagirs
Mansabdars were appointed as village accountants
Revenue was transferred directly to the imperial treasury
Jagirs became hereditary in the home territories of chiefs
133.x: Bejagiri meant that mansabdars remained without jagir assignments. It bred discontent and factionalism at the imperial court.
133.tq: Discriminate between a condition of non-assignment and the normal jagir arrangement.
133.sec: Transfer of jagirs and bejagiri - effects on nobility

133.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Tashiha — verification and muster of troops and horses
Chehra — descriptive roll of a trooper
Dagh — preparation of revenue papers by the assistant to the amalguzar
133.x: Dagh was the branding of horses to prevent substitution. Preparation of revenue papers and accounts was the duty of the Bitikchi.
133.tq: Find the one pair that belongs to a different administrative function.
133.sec: TERMS - dagh, chehra, tashiha and muster rules

133.s: Which statement regarding the Mughal muster system is correct?
o: The Qanungo conducted musters and imposed fines on zamindars
Musters were conducted by the provincial Diwan and failure resulted in loss of hereditary rights
Periodic musters were held under the Mir Bakhshi, and failure to present the required sawars could lead to pay cuts
The Kotwal verified only the land records of the pargana
133.x: Periodic military musters were conducted under the Mir Bakhshi. If the required sawars were not presented, the mansabdar could suffer pay cuts.
133.tq: Match the responsible authority with the precise consequence of non-compliance.
133.sec: TERMS - dagh, chehra, tashiha and muster rules

133.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Official)
 a. Amalguzar
 b. Karkun
 c. Qanungo
 d. Patwari

List-II (Duty)
 i. Village accountant
 ii. Keeper of pargana land and revenue records
 iii. District revenue collector
 iv. Accountant or clerk recording cultivation and revenue

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
133.x: The Amalguzar collected district revenue; the Karkun recorded cultivation and revenue; the Qanungo maintained pargana records; and the Patwari was the village accountant.
133.tq: Begin with the clear district and village offices, then complete the code.

133.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Bitikchi — assistant to the amalguzar who prepared revenue papers and accounts
Muqaddam — keeper of pargana revenue records
133.x: The Bitikchi assisted the Amalguzar and prepared revenue papers and accounts. The Khazanadar was the treasurer, the Chaudhari was a pargana-level revenue collector, and the Muqaddam was a village headman.
133.tq: Use the level and function of each official to reject swapped offices.

133.s: In the Mughal provincial hierarchy, the correct ascending order was:
133.x: The administrative order from the lowest to the highest level was village, pargana, sarkar and subah.
133.tq: Arrange administrative units from the smallest to the largest.
133.sec: Provincial set-up in ascending order and officials

133.s: Chakla in the Mughal administrative system was:
o: A group of villages below the pargana level
The imperial treasury attached to a subah
A military unit under the Mir Bakhshi
A group of parganas situated between the pargana and sarkar levels
133.x: A Chakla was a group of parganas placed between the pargana and sarkar levels. This arrangement dates from the time of Shah Jahan.
133.tq: Test the intermediate position of a lesser-known administrative unit.
133.sec: Provincial set-up in ascending order and officials

133.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the number of subahs:
1. Akbar established 12 subahs in 1580.
2. The number increased to 15 by the end of Akbar’s reign.
3. Aurangzeb had 21 subahs, with Golconda being the twenty-first.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
133.x: All three statements are correct: Akbar had 12 subahs in 1580, 15 by the end of his reign, and Aurangzeb had 21, with Golconda as the twenty-first.
133.tq: Check each date and count independently before selecting the coded combination.
133.sec: Provincial set-up in ascending order and officials

133.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Faujdar — military and law-and-order duties at the sarkar level
Subahdar — governor responsible for law and order
Provincial Diwan — revenue administration and an independent check on the governor
Kotwal — maintenance of pargana land and revenue records
133.x: The Kotwal was responsible for law and order in the city. Maintenance of land and revenue records at the pargana level was the duty of the Qanungo.
133.tq: Locate the wrong administrative level attached to the official.
133.sec: Provincial set-up in ascending order and officials

133.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Administrative level)
 a. Subah
 b. City
 c. Sarkar
 d. Pargana

List-II (Principal official or officials)
 i. Kotwal
 ii. Faujdar and Amalguzar
 iii. Shiqdar, Amil, Qanungo and Chaudhari
 iv. Subahdar, provincial Diwan, Bakhshi, Sadr and Qazi

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
133.x: The subah had the Subahdar and other provincial officers; the city had the Kotwal; the sarkar had the Faujdar and Amalguzar; and the pargana had the Shiqdar, Amil, Qanungo and Chaudhari.
133.tq: Match each office with its administrative level before comparing the codes.
133.sec: Provincial set-up in ascending order and officials

133.s: Which of the following correctly describes the relationship between the Subahdar and the provincial Diwan?
o: The Diwan commanded the imperial cavalry and the Subahdar maintained village accounts
The Subahdar handled provincial governance and law and order, while the Diwan managed revenue and acted as an independent check on the governor
The Subahdar maintained only revenue records, while the Diwan was the city police officer
Both were identical offices, with the Diwan subordinate to the Subahdar in all matters
133.x: The Subahdar was the provincial governor responsible for law and order. The provincial Diwan handled revenue and provided an independent check on the governor.
133.tq: Distinguish parallel provincial authorities by their functions and checking relationship.
133.sec: Provincial set-up in ascending order and officials

133.s: The official primarily responsible for military and police functions at the pargana level was the:
133.x: The Shiqdar performed military and police functions at the pargana level.
133.tq: Identify the office by matching the function with the correct administrative tier.
133.sec: Provincial set-up in ascending order and officials

133.s:
Which of the following statements about Mughal intelligence arrangements is correct?
1. Waqia-navis reported provincial events to the imperial court.
2. Khufia-navis and harkaras supplemented the news-writers.
3. Intelligence was under the Mir Bakhshi.
4. Sher Shah had already established an efficient espionage system.
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
133.x: All four statements are correct. Waqia-navis, khufia-navis and harkaras formed complementary channels, intelligence came under the Mir Bakhshi, and Sher Shah had earlier operated an efficient espionage system.
133.tq: Verify each component of the intelligence network before choosing the complete combination.

133.s: What was the principal political significance of the Mughal mansab-jagir system?
o: It separated the nobility completely from the emperor
It replaced all military assignments with hereditary offices
It restricted nobles to purely civil functions
It bound the nobility to the emperor
133.x: The mansab-jagir system bound the Mughal nobility to the emperor and helped maintain imperial control over them.
133.tq: Test the central significance directly by distinguishing the correct cause from reversed effects.

133.s: The breakdown of which system is regarded as a core explanation of the decline of the Mughal Empire?
133.x: The breakdown of the jagirdari system, known as the jagirdari crisis, is a core explanation of Mughal decline.
133.tq: Identify the exact system linked with the stated historical consequence.

133.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Mughal jagir and comparable administrative systems:
1. The Mughal jagir is compared with the Sultanate iqta.
2. The Mughal jagir is compared with the Kakatiya Nayankara system.
3. The Mughal jagir was identical to the British ICS in being purely civil and cash-paid.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
133.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct comparisons. Statement 3 is false because the British ICS was purely civil and cash-paid, whereas Mughal mansabdars performed mixed civil-military duties and were paid through jagirs.
133.tq: Find the wrong comparison by checking whether the paired systems are genuinely alike or merely comparable.

133.s: Which one of the following best distinguishes Mughal mansabdars from members of the British Indian Civil Service?
o: Mansabdars were purely civil officials paid fixed cash salaries, whereas the ICS performed mixed civil and military duties.
Mansabdars performed mixed civil and military duties and were paid in jagirs, whereas the ICS was purely civil and paid fixed cash salaries.
Both mansabdars and ICS officers performed mixed civil and military duties and were paid in jagirs.
Both systems were purely military and depended on hereditary appointments.
133.x: Mansabdars combined civil and military functions and received jagirs. The British ICS was purely civil and its officers received fixed cash salaries.
133.tq: Use a direct contrast to separate two similar administrative institutions.

133.s: A historian is comparing the Sultanate iqta, the Kakatiya Nayankara arrangement and the Mughal jagir. Which conclusion is supported by this comparison?
o: The Mughal jagir is treated as comparable to both the Sultanate iqta and the Kakatiya Nayankara system.
The Mughal jagir is presented as unrelated to both earlier systems.
The Mughal jagir is described as identical to the British ICS.
The Mughal jagir is described only as a village-level institution.
133.x: The Mughal jagir is compared with both the Sultanate iqta and the Kakatiya Nayankara system; it is not equated with the purely civil British ICS.
133.tq: Apply the comparative relationship to a historical classification problem.

133.s: Which of the following states retained a Mughal-style jagirdari administration?
o: Qutb Shahi state of Golconda only
133.x: The Asaf Jahi state of Hyderabad retained a Mughal-style jagirdari administration.
133.tq: Use the regional application angle to identify the state associated with the administrative practice.

133.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Office)
 a. Peshwa
 b. Mir Jumla
 c. Ain-ul-Mulk
 d. Majumdar

List-II (Function)
 i. Auditor
 ii. Military affairs
 iii. Finance
 iv. Peshwa

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
133.x: In Qutb Shahi Golconda, the Peshwa was the Peshwa, Mir Jumla handled finance, Ain-ul-Mulk handled military affairs and the Majumdar was the auditor.
133.tq: Start from the sure office-function pair and eliminate codes with swapped responsibilities.

133.s: During the rule of Tana Shah, the Qutb Shahi administration comprised:
133.x: Under Tana Shah, the Qutb Shahi administration had 37 sarkars and 517 parganas.
133.tq: Separate the two administrative counts and reject options that alter either figure.

133.s: In the village administration of Qutb Shahi Golconda, the offices of Mukaddam and Kulkarni were associated with the:
133.x: Mukaddam and Kulkarni were village-level officials in the Qutb Shahi administration of Golconda.
133.tq: Identify the administrative level attached to the named local offices.

133.s: Which of the following pairs correctly represents an institutional feature that contributed to the Mughal administrative model?
o: Sher Shah's pargana arrangement—Amin and Shiqdar
Sher Shah's pargana arrangement—Peshwa and Majumdar
133.x: Sher Shah's pargana set-up included the Amin and Shiqdar. The other offices listed belonged to the Qutb Shahi or village administrative context.
133.tq: Use the office-group association to detect the swapped institutional pair.

133.s: Which of the following pairs of Sultanate ministries is correctly matched?
133.x: The Sultanate ministries of Wazir and Diwan-i-Arz contributed to the Mughal administrative model, with the latter associated with military affairs.
133.tq: Match each office with its broad administrative sphere and avoid swapped authority traps.

134.s: Which one of the following officials functioned as the revenue collector at the Sarkar level in the Mughal administration?
134.x: The Amalguzar, also called the Amil, was responsible for the assessment and collection of revenue at the Sarkar level.
134.tq: Match the official with the level and duty before considering the distractors.

134.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Bitikchi — Accountant at the Sarkar level
2. Karkun — Clerk-writer at the Pargana level
3. Qanungo — Keeper of hereditary land records
4. Chaudhari — Village headman
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
134.x: Bitikchi, Karkun and Qanungo are correctly matched. Chaudhari was a Pargana-level revenue collector and local notable, not the village headman.
134.tq: Use the administrative level as the key to eliminate the swapped official-duty pair.

134.s: The official who maintained village accounts in the Mughal revenue administration was the
134.x: The Patwari was the village accountant. The Muqaddam was the village headman, while the Karkun worked at the Pargana level.
134.tq: Test the precise village-level function rather than the broader revenue hierarchy.

134.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Muqaddam — Village headman and revenue collector
Khazanadar — Keeper of hereditary land records
134.x: The Muqaddam, or Patel, was the village headman and collected revenue. The Khazanadar or Fotadar was the treasurer at the Sarkar level.
134.tq: Check whether the official is placed at the correct administrative level before accepting the duty.

134.s: The treasurer at the Sarkar level was known as the
134.x: Khazanadar and Fotadar were designations for the treasurer at the Sarkar level.
134.tq: Discriminate between treasury, revenue collection and auditing offices.

134.s: Which of the following combinations correctly represents the principal heads of a Mughal Suba and Sarkar respectively?
o: Subedar and provincial Diwan; Faujdar and Amalguzar
Shiqdar and Amil; Muqaddam and Patwari
Faujdar and Qanungo; Kotwal and Bakhshi
Amalguzar and Fotadar; Sadr and Qazi
134.x: A Suba was headed by the Subedar and provincial Diwan, while a Sarkar had the Faujdar and Amalguzar as its principal officials.
134.tq: Split the option into two administrative levels and verify both pairs.
134.sec: Units - suba, sarkar, chakla, pargana, village

134.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the Chakla is correct?
o: It was a unit between the Suba and Pargana and was prominent in Bengal under Murshid Quli Khan.
It was a military rank assigned to a Mansabdar.
It was identical with the Sarkar in every province.
It was the smallest village-level revenue unit.
134.x: Chakla was a unit between the Suba and Pargana, but it was not identical with the Sarkar. It was prominent in Bengal under Murshid Quli Khan.
134.tq: Separate the similar territorial terms Chakla and Sarkar by their exact position in the hierarchy.
134.sec: Units - suba, sarkar, chakla, pargana, village

134.s: Akbar initially organised the Mughal Empire into how many Subas?
134.x: Akbar began with 12 Subas. The number rose to 21 under Aurangzeb, when Golconda became the twenty-first Suba.
134.tq: Distinguish the initial and later numerical stages of provincial organisation.
134.sec: Units - suba, sarkar, chakla, pargana, village

134.s: Under Aurangzeb, the number of Subas reached 21 when which territory became the twenty-first Suba?
134.x: Golconda became the twenty-first Suba under Aurangzeb.
134.tq: Link the numerical change to the specific territorial addition.
134.sec: Units - suba, sarkar, chakla, pargana, village

134.s: Which one of the following best describes the extent of effective Mughal state reach in rural administration?
o: It was confined to the provincial capital and did not reach the Pargana.
It extended uniformly to every village through imperial officials.
It ended at the Sarkar, leaving Parganas independent.
It effectively ended at the Pargana, while villages were largely self-governing.
134.x: The state's effective administrative reach generally ended at the Pargana; villages retained substantial self-government.
134.tq: Apply the hierarchy to distinguish formal territorial division from effective administrative reach.
134.sec: Units - suba, sarkar, chakla, pargana, village

134.s: The provincial Diwan in the Mughal administration was independent of the Subedar primarily because he
o: controlled the city police and markets
served as a check on the Subedar in revenue and finance
134.x: The provincial Diwan handled revenue and finance independently of the Subedar, thereby acting as a check on the governor.
134.tq: Ask which official performed the balancing or checking function rather than the executive function.

134.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Bakhshi — Military pay and musters
2. Faujdar — Sarkar-level military command and law and order
3. Kotwal — City police, markets and watch on newcomers
4. Waqia-navis — News-writer reporting events to the centre
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
134.x: All four pairs are correctly matched. The Bakhshi also prepared news reports, while the Waqia-navis reported events to the centre.
134.tq: Verify each official against the distinctive function associated with the office.

134.s: Which of the following officials was responsible for salaries, known as tankhwah, and jagir assignments?
134.x: The Diwan-i-Tan dealt with salaries or tankhwah and jagir assignments. The Mustaufi was the auditor.
134.tq: Use the meaning of the office’s specialised financial responsibility to identify it.

134.s: The official who audited accounts in the Mughal administrative system was the
134.x: The Mustaufi was the auditor in the Mughal administrative structure.
134.tq: Distinguish audit from salary, military and judicial functions.

134.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Sadr — Grants and justice at provincial level
134.x: The Faujdar was responsible for Sarkar-level military command and law and order. The Mustaufi, not the Faujdar, was the auditor.
134.tq: Find the official whose function belongs to a different administrative category.

134.s: A Mansabdar receiving payment through a tankhwah jagir was connected to revenue collection in which sequence?
o: Mansabdar — Tankhwah jagir — Jagirdar's agents — Zamindars — Peasant
134.x: The Mansabdar received a rank and was paid through a tankhwah jagir; the jagirdar's agents collected assessed revenue through zamindars, from whom the peasant paid the state demand.
134.tq: Trace the institutional flow from rank and assignment to local collection and peasant payment.

134.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Jagirdars were generally transferred often and their assignments were not hereditary.
2. Zamindars were local figures who could maintain armed retainers.
3. Jagirdars were necessarily outsiders to the area of their assignment.
4. Zamindars helped in policing and revenue collection.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
134.x: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. The general distinction was that Jagirdars were outsiders to the area, whereas Zamindars were local; therefore statement 3 is incorrectly framed as a statement about Jagirdars without the institutional distinction being properly applied.
134.tq: Check each statement against the local-versus-outsider and hereditary-versus-transferable contrast.

134.s: In the Mughal revenue system, the peasant generally paid approximately what share of the produce?
134.x: The peasant's payment was approximately one-third of the produce in the mansabdar-jagirdar-zamindar revenue linkage.
134.tq: Retain the approximate fraction and reject nearby conventional revenue shares.

134.s: Which of the following was a major local manifestation of the jagirdari crisis?
o: Zamindars became salaried imperial officials and peasants received remissions permanently.
The state abolished revenue collection through local intermediaries.
Short-tenure Jagirdars pressed for more revenue, zamindars resisted or rebelled, and peasants fled.
Jagirdars reduced demands and zamindars abandoned cultivation.
134.x: Short tenure encouraged Jagirdars to press for higher collections; Zamindars resisted or rebelled, and peasants sometimes fled, producing a local face of the jagirdari crisis.
134.tq: Identify the connected cause-and-effect chain rather than an isolated symptom.

134.s: Raja Todar Mal is associated with which Mughal revenue arrangement?
o: Zabti or Bandobast, also called the Dahsala system
Iqtadari system based exclusively on military fiefs
Permanent Settlement based on zamindari ownership
134.x: Raja Todar Mal developed the Zabti or Bandobast system, also known as Dahsala, under Akbar.
134.tq: Associate the revenue reformer with the exact name of the system, not a neighbouring arrangement.
134.sec: Land revenue - zabti/dahsala, batai, kankut, nasaq; Todar Mal

134.s: Which statement regarding Raja Todar Mal is correct?
o: He served Aurangzeb and had earlier served Murshid Quli Khan.
He served only the Qutb Shahis and introduced the Pargana system.
He was a provincial Qazi who designed the Mansabdari system.
He served Akbar and had earlier served Sher Shah.
134.x: Todar Mal was Akbar's revenue minister and had earlier served Sher Shah. His system was modelled on Sher Shah's survey-based arrangements.
134.tq: Use the predecessor-service link to distinguish Todar Mal from other administrative figures.
134.sec: Land revenue - zabti/dahsala, batai, kankut, nasaq; Todar Mal

134.s: Under the Zabti or Dahsala system, the state share was generally calculated as
o: One-fourth of the village's previous revenue record
A fixed sum unrelated to measurement or average produce
One-half of the current year's standing crop, paid only in kind
One-third of the average produce of the last ten years, converted into cash
134.x: Under Zabti/Dahsala, land was measured and the state share was one-third of the average produce of the preceding ten years, commuted into cash as damil.
134.tq: Break the revenue formula into period, proportion and mode of payment.
134.sec: Land revenue - zabti/dahsala, batai, kankut, nasaq; Todar Mal

134.s: Which method involved dividing the actual crop between the state and the peasant?
134.x: Batai, also called Ghalla-bakhshi, was the crop-sharing method in which the produce was divided between the state and the peasant.
134.tq: Distinguish crop sharing from estimation, past-record assessment and cash commutation.
134.sec: Land revenue - zabti/dahsala, batai, kankut, nasaq; Todar Mal

134.s: The Kankut method of assessment was based on
o: Estimation of the standing crop by eye or sample
A measured ten-year average converted into cash
Division of the harvested crop into equal shares
A rough estimate from the village's past revenue record
134.x: Kankut involved estimating the standing crop through visual inspection or sample-based assessment.
134.tq: Identify the assessment method from the operational act used to estimate the crop.
134.sec: Land revenue - zabti/dahsala, batai, kankut, nasaq; Todar Mal

134.s: Nasaq differed from Kankut because Nasaq was based on
o: A visual estimate of the standing crop
The average produce of the previous ten years only
A division of the harvested crop between state and peasant
134.x: Nasaq was a rough assessment based on the village's past revenue record, whereas Kankut estimated the standing crop by eye or sample.
134.tq: Separate the two similar assessment methods by asking whether the basis was a record or the standing crop.
134.sec: Land revenue - zabti/dahsala, batai, kankut, nasaq; Todar Mal

134.s: Which one of the following statements is correct regarding Mughal revenue measurement and relief?
o: The Gaz-i-Ilahi was about 82 centimetres, bamboo rods were used, and taccavi loans and famine remissions were available.
The Gaz-i-Ilahi was a coin, and famine relief was provided only through military jagirs.
Taccavi referred to the commutation of produce into cash.
Measurement was made exclusively with iron chains and no loans were granted.
134.x: The Gaz-i-Ilahi measured about 82 cm; bamboo rods were used for measurement. Taccavi loans and remissions were measures of assistance during famine.
134.tq: Combine the measurement figure with the associated administrative relief measures.
134.sec: Land revenue - zabti/dahsala, batai, kankut, nasaq; Todar Mal

134.s:
Arrange the following land categories from the shortest to the longest period of fallow or uncultivated condition:
A. Banjar
B. Parauti
C. Polaj
D. Chachar
134.x: Polaj was cultivated every year, Parauti was fallow for one or two years, Chachar for three or four years, and Banjar was uncultivated for five or more years.
134.tq: Convert each land category into its time condition and then arrange the periods.
134.sec: Land classification - polaj, parauti, chachar, banjar

134.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Parauti — Fallow for one or two years
Chachar — Fallow for three or four years
134.x: Banjar referred to land left uncultivated for five or more years. Land fallow for two years was Parauti.
134.tq: Use the numerical duration attached to each land category to identify the mismatch.
134.sec: Land classification - polaj, parauti, chachar, banjar

134.s: Which category of zamindars consisted of Rajas ruling their own territories, paying tribute and serving as Mansabdars?
134.x: Autonomous chiefs were Rajas who ruled their own territories, paid tribute and could serve as Mansabdars.
134.tq: Match the political status and obligations with the correct zamindar category.

134.s: Intermediary zamindars were primarily responsible for
o: Serving as city police chiefs and regulating markets
Auditing provincial accounts independently of the Diwan
Collecting revenue from primary zamindars for the state and receiving a commission
134.x: Intermediary zamindars collected revenue from primary zamindars on behalf of the state and received a commission for the service.
134.tq: Distinguish collection through intermediaries from ownership and sovereign rule.

134.s: Primary zamindars were characterised by
o: Proprietary and hereditary rights over cultivated land
Non-hereditary assignments transferable at the pleasure of the emperor
Exclusive control over provincial military pay
134.x: Primary zamindars possessed proprietary, hereditary rights over cultivated land. This distinguished them from non-hereditary Jagirdars.
134.tq: Compare hereditary proprietary rights with temporary revenue assignments.

134.s: Which of the following correctly states the institutional significance of the Mughal Subedar-Diwan arrangement and the Zabti system?
o: The Subedar-Diwan arrangement applied only to villages, while Zabti applied only to cities.
Both became models for later revenue administration.
Both abolished the distinction between military and revenue offices.
Neither had influence beyond the Mughal provincial system.
134.x: The separation of the Subedar and Diwan and the Zabti revenue system were important models for later revenue administration.
134.tq: Identify the stated long-term significance rather than the immediate office function.

134.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched with the earlier or later administrative institution?
o: Sultanate Iqta — Kotwal; British district — hereditary zamindari only
Sultanate Shiq — Diwan-i-Tan; British district — village self-government alone
Sultanate Iqta — Muqti; British district — combined revenue, magisterial and police powers
Sultanate Pargana — Mansabdar; British district — separated revenue and police powers like the Mughals
134.x: The Sultanate had Iqtas administered by Muqtis, while the British district collector combined revenue, magisterial and police powers that the Mughals kept separate.
134.tq: Compare the institutional terms and the combination or separation of powers across periods.

134.s: Which of the following correctly represents the Qutb Shahi administrative arrangement in Golconda?
o: It followed the British district collector system of combined powers.
It had tarafs and simalu or se columns, with 37 Sarkars and 517 Parganas under Tana Shah.
It had only Subas and Sarkars, with 21 provinces under Tana Shah.
It abolished Parganas and placed all revenue under village Panchayats.
134.x: Qutb Shahi Golconda was organised into tarafs and simalu or seamas. Under Tana Shah it had 37 Sarkars and 517 Parganas.
134.tq: Check both the territorial terminology and the numerical composition before selecting the option.

134.s: In Qutb Shahi Golconda, which combination of village and Pargana officials is correctly matched?
o: Village Mukaddam and Kulkarni; Pargana Desai
Village Desai and Qazi; Pargana Kotwal
Village Amalguzar and Faujdar; Pargana Patwari
Village Subedar and Diwan; Pargana Muqaddam
134.x: The village officials included the Mukaddam and accountant Kulkarni, while the Desai served as the Pargana accounts officer.
134.tq: Separate village offices from the Pargana accounts office by administrative level.

134.s: Which statement regarding revenue collection in Qutb Shahi Golconda and the Northern Circars is correct?
o: Revenue was farmed out by auction, and Northern Circars zamindars date from the Qutb Shahi era.
Revenue was assessed exclusively through the Dahsala system, and Northern Circars had no zamindars.
Revenue was collected only through hereditary Mughal Jagirdars, and Northern Circars zamindars began under the British.
Revenue was collected by village Panchayats without intermediary rights.
134.x: In Qutb Shahi Golconda, revenue was farmed out through auction. Zamindars in the Northern Circars trace their origin to the Qutb Shahi era.
134.tq: Link the regional revenue practice with the historical origin of the local zamindars.

135.s: Which class of traders specialised in long-distance trade during the Mughal period?
135.x: Seths and Bohras specialised in long-distance trade. Baniks were local retail traders, while mahajans were moneylenders-cum-merchants.
135.tq: Distinguish trader classes by their specialised function.
135.sec: Trader classes - function (banjaras, beoparis, sarrafs, mahajans, baniks)

135.s: Baniks in the Mughal period were primarily engaged in which activity?
o: Long-distance transport of grain on oxen
135.x: Baniks were local or retail traders. The other functions belonged to transporters, sarrafs or revenue officials.
135.tq: Match the occupational title with its specific commercial function.
135.sec: Trader classes - function (banjaras, beoparis, sarrafs, mahajans, baniks)

135.s:
Consider the following statements about beoparis:
1. They dealt in commodities.
2. They often purchased agricultural produce from villages.
3. They were primarily money-changers and bankers.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
135.x: Beoparis were traders or dealers in commodities and often bought produce from villages. Money-changing and banking were functions of sarrafs.
135.tq: Find the one wrongly assigned occupational function.
135.sec: Trader classes - function (banjaras, beoparis, sarrafs, mahajans, baniks)

135.s: Which one of the following was NOT a function of the sarrafs or shroffs?
135.x: Sarrafs tested coins, took deposits and issued hundis. Cultivation was not a function of this banking and money-changing class.
135.tq: Identify the occupational function that does not belong to the group.
135.sec: Trader classes - function (banjaras, beoparis, sarrafs, mahajans, baniks)

135.s: The term ‘mahajans’ in the Mughal commercial context referred to
o: Carriers of bulk goods on oxen
135.x: Mahajans functioned as moneylenders-cum-merchants. They were distinct from baniks, who were local retail traders.
135.tq: Use a precise occupational definition rather than a broad trade association.
135.sec: Trader classes - function (banjaras, beoparis, sarrafs, mahajans, baniks)

135.s:
Consider the following statements regarding merchant communities in the Mughal period:
1. Merchant communities cut across religious boundaries.
2. Gujarati merchants included Hindus, Jains and Muslims.
3. Trading communities were generally unorganised and lacked professional specialisation.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
135.x: Merchant communities crossed religious boundaries, and Gujarati merchants included Hindus, Jains and Muslims. Trading classes were numerous, organised and highly professional, so statement 3 is false.
135.tq: Reject the extreme negative description that reverses a comparative social characteristic.
135.sec: Trader classes - function (banjaras, beoparis, sarrafs, mahajans, baniks)

135.s: Which of the following groups constituted the Marwaris mentioned in the context of Indian commerce?
135.x: The Marwaris included the Oswals, Maheshwaris and Agarwals of Rajasthan.
135.tq: Recall a named community through its constituent groups.
135.sec: Trader classes - function (banjaras, beoparis, sarrafs, mahajans, baniks)

135.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Community)
 a. Marwaris
 b. Chettis
 c. Muslim merchants
 d. Gujarati merchants

List-II (Association)
 i. Included Hindus, Jains and Muslims
 ii. Dominated Malabar trade
 iii. Oswals, Maheshwaris and Agarwals
 iv. Merchants of the Coromandel coast

Which of the following is the correct answer?
135.x: Marwaris comprised Oswals, Maheshwaris and Agarwals; Chettis were Coromandel merchants; Muslim merchants dominated Malabar trade; and Gujarati merchants included Hindus, Jains and Muslims.
135.tq: Start from the sure community–region pair and eliminate the codes.
135.sec: Trader classes - function (banjaras, beoparis, sarrafs, mahajans, baniks)

135.s: The Chettis were traditionally associated with trade on the
135.x: Chettis were merchants of the Coromandel coast in South India.
135.tq: Discriminate between closely associated coastal trading communities.
135.sec: Trader classes - function (banjaras, beoparis, sarrafs, mahajans, baniks)

135.s: Who was the head of a merchant community and dealt with government officials?
135.x: The nagarseth was the head of a merchant community and acted as its representative in dealings with officials.
135.tq: Identify the institutional representative from a group of related administrative terms.
135.sec: Trader classes - function (banjaras, beoparis, sarrafs, mahajans, baniks)

135.s: Merchant strikes are specifically recorded in the historical context of
135.x: Merchant strikes are recorded in Ahmedabad, illustrating the collective organisation of trading communities.
135.tq: Link a social-economic practice with its specifically mentioned location.
135.sec: Trader classes - function (banjaras, beoparis, sarrafs, mahajans, baniks)

135.s: Which of the following correctly describes the earlier Sultanate pattern of commercial control?
o: Overseas trade was controlled exclusively by Chettis, while inland trade was controlled by European companies.
Overseas trade was controlled by Baniks, while inland trade was controlled by Khurasanis alone.
Overseas trade was controlled by Multanis and Khurasanis, while inland trade involved Gujarati, Marwari and Muslim Bohra merchants.
Both overseas and inland trade were controlled by sarrafs alone.
135.x: In the earlier Sultanate pattern, Multanis and Khurasanis controlled overseas trade, whereas Gujarati, Marwari and Muslim Bohra merchants were important in inland trade.
135.tq: Separate the groups associated with overseas and inland trade instead of treating them as identical.
135.sec: Trader classes - function (banjaras, beoparis, sarrafs, mahajans, baniks)

135.s: Approximately what proportion of rural agricultural produce reached the market during the Mughal period?
135.x: Approximately 15 percent of rural agricultural produce reached the market. The pressure to pay revenue in cash encouraged peasants to sell produce.
135.tq: Recall the approximate quantitative share and reject inflated estimates.
135.sec: Rural produce marketed - share and commercial crops

135.s: The Mughal term ‘jins-i-kamil’, meaning ‘perfect crops’, referred to
o: Crops reserved exclusively for royal kitchens
135.x: Jins-i-kamil referred to commercial or superior cash crops such as cotton, sugarcane, indigo, oilseeds and opium.
135.tq: Distinguish the technical term for commercial crops from land classifications and imported crops.
135.sec: Rural produce marketed - share and commercial crops

135.s: Which one of the following was NOT included among the commercial crops mentioned in the Mughal context?
135.x: Cotton, indigo and opium were listed as commercial crops. Wheat was a staple crop rather than one of the specifically listed commercial crops in this classification.
135.tq: Find the item that belongs to the staple-crop group rather than the commercial-crop group.
135.sec: Rural produce marketed - share and commercial crops

135.s:
Consider the following statements about regional agricultural exports:
1. Gujarat exported indigo and food grains.
2. Bengal exported sugar and rice.
3. Bengal was particularly associated with the export of indigo rather than sugar and rice.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
135.x: Gujarat exported indigo and food grains, while Bengal was associated with sugar and rice. Statement 3 reverses the regional association and is false.
135.tq: Use regional comparison and detect the reversed export association.
135.sec: Rural produce marketed - share and commercial crops

135.s: Which of the following sets consists of crops that came to India through the Portuguese from the New World?
135.x: Tobacco, maize and chillies were New World crops introduced through the Portuguese route. Rice, wheat, sugarcane and the other listed crops were not the relevant set here.
135.tq: Identify the complete set by separating introduced crops from established Indian crops.
135.sec: Rural produce marketed - share and commercial crops

135.s: Which one of the following pairs consists of crops domesticated in the New World?
135.x: Tobacco, cocoa and rubber were domesticated in the New World; tobacco and cocoa therefore form a correct pair.
135.tq: Use the origin-of-crops distinction to eliminate Old World crops.
135.sec: Rural produce marketed - share and commercial crops

135.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Land category)
 a. Polaj
 b. Parauti
 c. Chachar
 d. Banjar

List-II (Condition of land)
 i. Uncultivated
 ii. Fallow for one year
 iii. Cultivated annually
 iv. Fallow for three to four years

Which of the following is the correct answer?
135.x: Polaj was cultivated annually; Parauti remained fallow for one year; Chachar for three to four years; and Banjar was uncultivated.
135.tq: Start with the familiar Polaj–annual cultivation pair and complete the land classification.
135.sec: Rural produce marketed - share and commercial crops

135.s: Under the Zabt system, the state share was fixed at
o: One-half of the produce of the current year
One-third of the average produce of the past ten years
One-fourth of the average produce of the preceding five years
One-sixth of the average produce of the preceding twelve years
135.x: The state share was one-third of the average produce calculated over the past ten years.
135.tq: Keep the fraction and reference period together while eliminating altered figures.
135.sec: Rural produce marketed - share and commercial crops

135.s:
Consider the following statements about the Zabt system:
1. Revenue was paid mainly in cash.
2. Patta and Qabuliyat were issued in connection with land revenue arrangements.
3. The system discouraged peasants from producing cash crops.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
135.x: Revenue was paid mainly in cash, and Patta and Qabuliyat were issued. Cash payment encouraged peasants to grow cash crops, so statement 3 is false.
135.tq: Identify the statement that reverses the cause-and-effect relationship.
135.sec: Rural produce marketed - share and commercial crops

135.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Patta — insurance contract; Qabuliyat — royal order
Patta — title deed; Qabuliyat — deed of agreement
Patta — cash receipt; Qabuliyat — land-measuring rod
Patta — merchant licence; Qabuliyat — military appointment
135.x: Patta was a title deed, while Qabuliyat was a deed of agreement issued in the revenue arrangement.
135.tq: Discriminate between two closely associated revenue documents.
135.sec: Rural produce marketed - share and commercial crops

135.s: Which one of the following was NOT listed among the cash crops and staples associated with Mughal agriculture?
135.x: Rice, pepper and spices were included among the listed cash crops and staples. Tobacco was mentioned separately as a New World crop introduced through the Portuguese.
135.tq: Separate a crop mentioned in a different context from the specified agricultural list.
135.sec: Rural produce marketed - share and commercial crops

135.s: The Shahab Nahr was built by restoring which earlier canal?
135.x: The Shahab Nahr was constructed by restoring the Rajabwah canal of Firuz Shah.
135.tq: Match a later irrigation work with the earlier canal it restored.
135.sec: Rural produce marketed - share and commercial crops

135.s: Which of the following best describes agriculture in the eighteenth century in the context under consideration?
o: It was fully mechanised and free from intermediary demands.
It was stagnant and technologically backward, while peasants paid several layers of authority.
It became technologically advanced after the complete abolition of revenue farming.
It expanded rapidly because peasants paid revenue only to the emperor.
135.x: By the eighteenth century agriculture was stagnant and technologically backward. Peasants had to pay the state, zamindars, jagirdars and revenue-farmers.
135.tq: Reject absolute improvement claims and identify the complete chain of revenue demands.
135.sec: Rural produce marketed - share and commercial crops

135.s: A merchant deposits cash with a shroff and receives a document enabling the amount to be collected at another place after a journey. This document is known as
135.x: A hundi was a letter of credit issued by a shroff against cash deposited at one place and encashed later or elsewhere. A farman was a royal order and rokad denoted cash.
135.tq: Apply the functional definition to distinguish a credit instrument from nearby terms.
135.sec: Credit instruments - hundi, bima, shroffs

135.s: Which one of the following correctly describes bima in the Mughal commercial system?
o: Insurance of goods in transit against a premium
A cash receipt issued by a banik
A royal order issued by the emperor
A land deed issued under the Zabt system
135.x: Bima was insurance for goods in transit, underwritten by sarrafs for a premium.
135.tq: Distinguish insurance terminology from credit and revenue documents.
135.sec: Credit instruments - hundi, bima, shroffs

135.s:
Consider the following statements about shroffs:
1. They operated the credit network.
2. They acted as money-changers, deposit keepers and lenders.
3. They were exclusively transporters of bulk goods.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
135.x: Shroffs ran the credit network and acted as money-changers, deposit keepers and lenders. Transporting bulk goods was associated with another trader class, not shroffs.
135.tq: Remove the statement that assigns a transport function to a financial class.
135.sec: Credit instruments - hundi, bima, shroffs

135.s: The English East India Company fitted into the existing Indian credit system through its reliance on
135.x: The English East India Company relied on Indian brokers or dalals, shroffs and banians and thus fitted into the existing credit network.
135.tq: Identify the institutional intermediaries that connected a foreign company to the indigenous credit system.
135.sec: Credit instruments - hundi, bima, shroffs

135.s:
Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes hundi from bima?
1. Hundi was a letter of credit.
2. Bima was insurance of goods in transit.
3. Both were issued as royal commands by the emperor.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
135.x: A hundi was a letter of credit, whereas bima insured goods in transit. Neither was a royal command issued by the emperor.
135.tq: Separate two similar commercial instruments and reject the wrong issuing authority.
135.sec: Credit instruments - hundi, bima, shroffs

135.s: Which of the following was NOT a function of sarrafs in the credit network?
135.x: Sarrafs issued hundis, kept deposits and could underwrite bima for a premium. Farmans were royal orders, not instruments issued by sarrafs.
135.tq: Use the wrong-authority trap to identify the non-financial function.
135.sec: Credit instruments - hundi, bima, shroffs

135.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Tapan Raychaudhuri — Co-editor of the Cambridge Economic History of India, Volume I
Tavernier — The Agrarian System of Mughal India, 1556-1707
135.x: Tapan Raychaudhuri was a co-editor, along with Irfan Habib, of the Cambridge Economic History of India, Volume I. Six Voyages was associated with Tavernier, Early Travels in India with William Foster, and Storia do Mogor with Niccolao Manucci.
135.tq: Use the author-work association and reject swapped authorship traps.
135.sec: Historians and travellers on the Mughal economy - books

135.s: Which of the following works is associated with J.B. Tavernier?
o: India at the Death of Akbar
135.x: J.B. Tavernier wrote Six Voyages, also referred to as Six Travels in India. The other works were associated with Bernier, William Foster and W.H. Moreland respectively.
135.tq: Distinguish closely related travel accounts by matching the traveller with the exact title.
135.sec: Historians and travellers on the Mughal economy - books

135.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Francois Bernier:
1. He was a French physician.
2. He served as the physician of Dara Shikoh.
3. He was patronised by Danishmand Khan.
4. He argued that the absence of private property in land contributed to agrarian ruin.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
135.x: All four statements are correct. Bernier was a French physician, served Dara Shikoh, was patronised by Danishmand Khan, and linked the absence of private landownership with agrarian deterioration.
135.tq: Check each biographical and analytical detail separately before selecting the complete combination.
135.sec: Historians and travellers on the Mughal economy - books

135.s: Bernier's observations on the Mughal economy included which one of the following combinations?
o: Private ownership of all land, agrarian prosperity and outflow of precious metals
Imperial ownership of land, agrarian ruin, inflow of precious metals and prosperity of merchants
Village ownership of land, decline of trade and absence of merchants
Merchant ownership of land, peasant prosperity and exclusive use of copper currency
135.x: Bernier believed that the emperor owned all land and blamed this arrangement for agrarian ruin. He nevertheless acknowledged that precious metals flowed into India and that merchants prospered.
135.tq: Separate the traveller's criticism of landholding from his observations on trade and precious-metal inflow.
135.sec: Historians and travellers on the Mughal economy - books

135.s: J.B. Tavernier was best known in the context of Mughal-period India as a
o: Dutch VOC merchant who spent seven years in Agra
English merchant who recorded a famine during Shah Jahan's reign
French diamond merchant who visited the diamond mines of Golconda
French physician who served Dara Shikoh
135.x: Tavernier was a French gem and diamond merchant who made six visits to India and described the diamond mines of Golconda. The other descriptions relate to Bernier, Pelsaert and Peter Mundy.
135.tq: Discriminate among European visitors by identifying profession and subject of observation.
135.sec: Historians and travellers on the Mughal economy - books

135.s: Which one of the following statements regarding Tavernier is correct?
o: He reached Surat in 1666 and visited the Qutb Shahi tombs.
He was an Italian doctor who wrote Storia do Mogor.
He visited India only once during Akbar's reign.
He made six visits and recorded the Koh-i-Noor from the Kollur mines.
135.x: Tavernier made six visits to India during the reigns of Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb and documented the Koh-i-Noor associated with the Kollur mines. The other options describe Manucci or Thevenot, or give an incorrect number and period of visits.
135.tq: Use the distinctive numerical detail and compare the traveller's identity with nearby European visitors.
135.sec: Historians and travellers on the Mughal economy - books

135.s: The Koh-i-Noor recorded by Tavernier was associated with which of the following?
o: The Golconda mines in Hyderabad and a weight of 40 carats
The Surat mines and a weight of 165 carats
The Kollur diamond mines in Guntur and a weight of 106 carats
The Agra mines and a weight of 178 grains
135.x: Tavernier recorded the Koh-i-Noor as a 106-carat diamond from the Kollur mines in Guntur. The other locations and measurements are not associated with this description.
135.tq: Combine the place and figure to avoid confusion between diamond details and coin weights.
135.sec: Historians and travellers on the Mughal economy - books

135.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Traveller)
A. Niccolao Manucci
B. Jean de Thevenot
C. Francisco Pelsaert
D. Peter Mundy

List-II (Description)
1. Dutch VOC merchant who came in 1620 and stayed seven years in Agra
2. English merchant who recorded a famine during Shah Jahan's reign
3. Italian doctor associated with the Mughal court and court intrigues after Shah Jahan
4. French traveller and physician who reached Surat in 1666

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
135.x: Manucci was the Italian doctor linked with court intrigues; Thevenot reached Surat in 1666; Pelsaert was the Dutch VOC merchant; and Peter Mundy was the English merchant who recorded a famine.
135.tq: Start with the distinctive nationality or profession and then complete the matching code.
135.sec: Historians and travellers on the Mughal economy - books

135.s: Jean de Thevenot's travels in India included visits to
135.x: Jean de Thevenot, a French traveller and physician, reached Surat in 1666 and visited Machilipatnam and Golconda. His account also referred to Hyderabad and the Qutb Shahi tombs.
135.tq: Use the travel itinerary as a location-based discrimination question.
135.sec: Historians and travellers on the Mughal economy - books

135.s:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
A. Sir Thomas Roe reached Jahangir's court.
B. Francisco Pelsaert came to India.
C. Peter Mundy travelled in India.
D. Jean de Thevenot reached Surat.

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
135.x: Sir Thomas Roe reached Jahangir's court in 1615, Pelsaert came in 1620, Peter Mundy travelled during 1630-34, and Thevenot reached Surat in 1666.
135.tq: Place the dated events first and then arrange the intervening travel accounts.
135.sec: Historians and travellers on the Mughal economy - books

135.s: Captain William Hawkins and Sir Thomas Roe are respectively associated with
o: Shah Jahan's reign at Agra and Aurangzeb's court in 1666
Akbar's reign at Fatehpur Sikri and Shah Jahan's court in 1630
Jahangir's reign at Surat and Jahangir's court in 1615
Aurangzeb's reign at Golconda and Jahangir's court in 1605
135.x: Captain William Hawkins came to Surat during Jahangir's reign, while Sir Thomas Roe visited Jahangir's court in 1615. The other combinations incorrectly assign their periods or locations.
135.tq: Distinguish two English visitors by pairing each with the correct Mughal setting and date.
135.sec: Historians and travellers on the Mughal economy - books

135.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Chalni — Coins of a previous reign accepted at a discount
135.x: Chalni referred to coins of the current reign in circulation. Coins of a previous reign accepted at a discount were called Khazana.
135.tq: Find the one reversed definition among the coin-metal and coin-status pairs.
135.sec: Coins - metal and name

135.s:
With reference to Mughal coinage, consider the following statements:
1. The rupiya was a silver coin standardised by Sher Shah.
2. Sher Shah's rupiya weighed 178 grains.
3. Akbar continued the silver rupiya standard.
4. The dam was a copper coin.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
135.x: All four statements are correct. The silver rupiya was standardised by Sher Shah at 178 grains, continued by Akbar, while the dam was made of copper.
135.tq: Combine the metal, standardiser, weight and continuation details before choosing the coded option.
135.sec: Coins - metal and name

135.s: How many dams were equivalent to one rupee in the Mughal monetary system?
135.x: Forty copper dams were equivalent to one rupee. The dam was the copper denomination, while the rupiya was the silver coin.
135.tq: Identify the exact conversion figure rather than confusing it with the coin's metal or name.
135.sec: Coins - metal and name

135.s: The term 'Sikka' in the Mughal monetary system denoted
o: the copper coin equal to one-fortieth of a rupee
the gold coin used for long-distance trade
coins of a previous reign accepted at a discount
the right of coinage in the ruler's name, signifying sovereignty along with the khutba
135.x: Sikka denoted the right of coinage in the ruler's name and, together with the khutba, symbolised sovereignty. The other options describe the dam, khazana and mohur respectively.
135.tq: Distinguish a political symbol of sovereignty from the names of actual coin denominations.
135.sec: Coins - metal and name

135.s: Which one of the following statements about coin circulation in the Deccan is correct?
o: Golconda minted only silver coins and prohibited copper currency.
Mughal silver coins circulated even in Golconda, while Golconda itself minted only copper coins.
Golconda circulated only gold coins and rejected Mughal silver coins.
Mughal coins circulated only in northern India and not in Golconda.
135.x: Mughal silver coins circulated in Golconda, although Golconda itself minted only copper coins, as noted by Thevenot.
135.tq: Use the contrast between circulation and local minting to reject reversed regional claims.
135.sec: Coins - metal and name

135.s: Which Mughal port was known as the ‘Gate of Mecca’ or Bab-ul-Makka because of its association with the Haj pilgrimage?
135.x: Surat was the chief Mughal port on the west coast and was known as the Gateway to Mecca or Bab-ul-Makka owing to its importance for Haj traffic.
135.tq: Use the port–epithet association directly.
135.sec: Ports and trading centres - epithets, exports, imports

135.s:
With reference to the early English presence in Mughal India, consider the following statements:
1. English ships reached Surat in 1608.
2. Hawkins obtained a firman in 1609.
3. Roe secured an English factory at Surat in 1615.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
135.x: All three statements are correct: English ships arrived at Surat in 1608, Hawkins obtained a firman in 1609, and Roe secured the factory in 1615.
135.tq: Check the chronological sequence of closely related dates.
135.sec: Ports and trading centres - epithets, exports, imports

135.s: Cambay, also known as Khambhat, declined principally because of which of the following?
o: Loss of its access to the Indus mouth
135.x: Cambay was an old Gujarat port whose importance declined because silting affected its harbour.
135.tq: Identify the specific cause attached to the port.
135.sec: Ports and trading centres - epithets, exports, imports

135.s: Which one of the following combinations relating to Masulipatnam is correct?
o: Old Gujarat port — Kashmiri shawl distribution
135.x: Masulipatnam was a Qutb Shahi or Golconda port and was noted for Kalamkari, also called chintz, textiles.
135.tq: Start from the sure port–trade pair.
135.sec: Ports and trading centres - epithets, exports, imports

135.s:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
A. Dutch factory at Masulipatnam
B. English factory at Masulipatnam
C. French presence at Masulipatnam
D. Shah Jahan’s expulsion of the Portuguese from Hugli
135.x: The Dutch arrived at Masulipatnam in 1605, the English in 1611, the Portuguese were expelled from Hugli in 1632, and the French arrived at Masulipatnam in 1669.
135.tq: Fix the earliest and latest dates first, then place the middle events.
135.sec: Ports and trading centres - epithets, exports, imports

135.s: Which of the following ports was a Portuguese base in Bengal until Shah Jahan expelled the Portuguese in 1632?
135.x: Hugli was the Portuguese settlement and base in Bengal; Shah Jahan expelled them in 1632.
135.tq: Apply the ruler–port association.
135.sec: Ports and trading centres - epithets, exports, imports

135.s: Lahari Bandar was located at which of the following places?
o: The mouth of the Indus in Sindh
The mouth of the Ganga in Bengal
135.x: Lahari Bandar was a port of Sindh situated at the mouth of the Indus.
135.tq: Use location-based discrimination among ports.
135.sec: Ports and trading centres - epithets, exports, imports

135.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Bengal — sugar, rice, muslin and silk
Gujarat — chiefly porcelain and war horses
135.x: Gujarat was an entry point for foreign goods and exported indigo and food grains; porcelain and war horses were imports, not its characteristic exports.
135.tq: Find the reversed export–import relationship.
135.sec: Ports and trading centres - epithets, exports, imports

135.s: Which of the following was an import into Mughal India rather than an export?
135.x: War horses were imported. Saltpetre, indigo and muslin were among the important exports.
135.tq: Separate the export list from the import list.
135.sec: Ports and trading centres - epithets, exports, imports

135.s: The Golden Firman of 1636, issued by Abdullah Qutb Shah, primarily granted which of the following?
o: The Dutch monopoly over Coromandel textiles
French exemption from all Mughal taxes
135.x: The Golden Firman of 1636, issued by Abdullah Qutb Shah, granted the English trade rights.
135.tq: Match the document with its issuer and beneficiary.
135.sec: Ports and trading centres - epithets, exports, imports

135.s:
Which of the following statements regarding European trade privileges is correct?
1. The English obtained duty exemptions from Shah Jahan in 1652.
2. The Dutch obtained duty exemptions from Shah Jahan in 1665.
3. Farrukhsiyar’s firman of 1716/1717 reduced English duties.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
135.x: All three statements are correct. Shah Jahan granted exemptions to the English in 1652 and the Dutch in 1665, while Farrukhsiyar’s firman of 1716/1717 reduced English duties.
135.tq: Test multiple dates and beneficiaries without reversing them.
135.sec: Ports and trading centres - epithets, exports, imports

135.s: Which of the following groups consists entirely of goods exported from Mughal India?
o: War horses, silver, porcelain and wine
135.x: Muslin, saltpetre, indigo and sugar were exports. The other groups contain goods listed as imports.
135.tq: Eliminate groups containing known imports.
135.sec: Ports and trading centres - epithets, exports, imports

135.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched with an important production or trading centre in Andhra Pradesh?
135.x: Saltpetre was associated with Machilipatnam, Narsapur and Pulicat. Damascus swords were associated with Nirmal or Indur, while carpets or durries were associated with Warangal.
135.tq: Distinguish neighbouring regional specialisations.
135.sec: Ports and trading centres - epithets, exports, imports

135.s: Who supervised the Mughal royal karkhanas?
135.x: The Mughal royal karkhanas were supervised by the Mir Saman, also known as Khan-i-Saman.
135.tq: Apply the ‘who would do this job?’ method.
135.sec: Karkhanas - royal workshops

135.s:
Consider the following statements about Mughal karkhanas:
1. They produced luxury goods for the court.
2. They manufactured gold and silver articles, fine textiles, arms and jewellery.
3. Their institutional tradition went back to the Sultanate period.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
135.x: All three statements are correct. Mughal karkhanas supplied courtly luxury goods and continued a tradition inherited from the Sultanate karkhanas.
135.tq: Combine the functions, products and historical continuity of an institution.
135.sec: Karkhanas - royal workshops

135.s: Which one of the following statements about artisans in the Mughal period is NOT correct?
o: They could work in private enterprises.
They could work in state karkhanas.
They were often organised into guilds.
They worked exclusively in royal karkhanas.
135.x: Artisans worked in both state karkhanas and private enterprises and were often organised into guilds; they were not confined exclusively to royal workshops.
135.tq: Reject the extreme ‘exclusively’ statement.
135.sec: Karkhanas - royal workshops

135.s: The expression ‘sink of precious metals’ in the context of early modern India refers to which of the following?
o: India’s export of all its silver coinage to Europe
India’s absorption of large quantities of imported gold and silver
The use of silver only in royal karkhanas
The replacement of silver by copper currency
135.x: India became a ‘sink of precious metals’ because European companies paid for Indian goods with bullion, causing large inflows of gold and silver.
135.tq: Translate the metaphor into its economic meaning.
135.sec: Silver influx and Indian Ocean commerce

135.s: The major source of the silver that reached India through European trade was the silver of which region?
135.x: Much of the silver came from Spanish America in the New World and reached India through Europe and the Pacific.
135.tq: Identify the source rather than the route.
135.sec: Silver influx and Indian Ocean commerce

135.s: Which traveller described silver as crossing the globe to reach India around 1690?
135.x: Careri, writing around 1690, described the global movement of silver to India. Bernier also commented on India’s export surplus and silver inflow.
135.tq: Discriminate between traveller–observation pairs.
135.sec: Silver influx and Indian Ocean commerce

135.s:
One important effect of the inflow of silver into India was:
1. An increase in silver rupee coinage.
2. A rise in prices.
3. The disappearance of bullion from Indian markets.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
135.x: The silver influx increased silver rupee coinage and contributed to a rise in prices. It did not cause bullion to disappear from Indian markets.
135.tq: Identify the true economic effects and reject the reversal.
135.sec: Silver influx and Indian Ocean commerce

135.s: Which of the following was NOT a merchant group engaged in Asian trade connected with India?
135.x: Gujaratis, Bohras and Chettis were Asian merchant groups. The Portuguese were a European trading group.
135.tq: Separate Asian merchant communities from European companies.
135.sec: Silver influx and Indian Ocean commerce

135.s: Which one of the following was a European trading group active in Indian Ocean commerce?
135.x: The English East India Company, founded in 1600, was one of the European trading groups active in Indian Ocean commerce.
135.tq: Classify the merchant group by region and institutional form.
135.sec: Silver influx and Indian Ocean commerce

135.s:
Arrange the following European trading companies in the order of the dates specifically associated with them:
A. English East India Company
B. Dutch trading presence at Masulipatnam
C. English trading presence at Masulipatnam
D. French trading presence at Masulipatnam
135.x: The English East India Company was established in 1600, the Dutch reached Masulipatnam in 1605, the English in 1611, and the French in 1669.
135.tq: Arrange the dates from the earliest institutional event to the latest port arrival.
135.sec: Silver influx and Indian Ocean commerce

135.s: India’s trade balance with overseas merchants generally remained favourable until which period?
o: The beginning of the seventeenth century
The beginning of the nineteenth century
The end of the fifteenth century
135.x: India’s trade balance remained favourable until the mid-eighteenth century.
135.tq: Select the precise chronological limit rather than a broad century label.
135.sec: Silver influx and Indian Ocean commerce

135.s: Which combination best explains the decline in India’s favourable trade balance after the mid-eighteenth century?
o: The expulsion of all European merchants from India
Silting of all Gujarat ports and the end of textile production
The disappearance of silver from Spanish America
Aurangzeb’s Deccan wars, insecurity and loss of Indian shipping
135.x: The decline was associated with Aurangzeb’s Deccan wars, growing insecurity and the loss of Indian shipping.
135.tq: Link the economic decline to its stated political and maritime causes.
135.sec: Silver influx and Indian Ocean commerce

135.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Pahi-kasht — cultivated land in the peasant’s own village
Khud-kasht — cultivated land in another village
Khud-kasht — cultivated land in the peasant’s own village
135.x: Khud-kasht peasants cultivated land in their own village, whereas pahi-kasht peasants cultivated land in another village.
135.tq: Discriminate between two closely related agrarian terms.
135.sec: Social classes - nobility, zamindars, peasants (khud-kasht, pahi-kasht), artisans

135.s:
Consider the following statements about Mughal social classes:
1. The nobility consisted of high mansabdars.
2. Turanis, Iranis, Hindustanis and Rajputs were represented among the nobility.
3. The nobility was wealthy but dependent on the Emperor’s favour.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
135.x: All three statements correctly describe the Mughal nobility or Umara.
135.tq: Test composition and political-economic status together.
135.sec: Social classes - nobility, zamindars, peasants (khud-kasht, pahi-kasht), artisans

135.s: Which of the following best describes the position of zamindars in Mughal rural society?
o: Royal artisans attached exclusively to karkhanas
Hereditary rural superior-right holders who received a large share with jagirdars and revenue-farmers
Temporary urban wage labourers without hereditary rights
Foreign merchants who controlled Indian Ocean shipping
135.x: Zamindars were hereditary rural superior-right holders and took a large share along with jagirdars and revenue-farmers.
135.tq: Distinguish the rural intermediary from urban and commercial groups.
135.sec: Social classes - nobility, zamindars, peasants (khud-kasht, pahi-kasht), artisans

135.s: Which of the following correctly represents the position of artisans and merchants in Mughal society?
o: They were confined to the imperial court and had no private enterprises.
They formed the hereditary rural superior-right-holding class.
They formed middle and lower urban strata and were associated with guilds and karkhanas.
They constituted the entire Mughal nobility.
135.x: Artisans and merchants constituted middle and lower urban strata and were associated with guilds and karkhanas.
135.tq: Match the social group with its location and institutions.
135.sec: Social classes - nobility, zamindars, peasants (khud-kasht, pahi-kasht), artisans

135.s: Which statement most accurately characterises eighteenth-century Mughal society?
o: It eliminated the distinction between peasants and nobility.
It was marked by uniform prosperity among all classes.
It was dominated entirely by artisan guilds.
It displayed extreme poverty alongside extreme wealth.
135.x: Eighteenth-century society was characterised by the coexistence of extreme poverty and extreme wealth.
135.tq: Identify the precise comparative description of society.
135.sec: Social classes - nobility, zamindars, peasants (khud-kasht, pahi-kasht), artisans

135.s: The Mughal economy has been described as significant for the East India Company because it was characterised by which of the following?
o: A subsistence economy based entirely on barter
A monetised, credit-backed economy with a trade surplus
A closed economy without overseas commerce
An economy dependent exclusively on imported bullion
135.x: The Mughal economy was monetised, supported by credit and marked by a trade surplus. These conditions provided the economic base from which the East India Company later built its power.
135.tq: Identify the precise economic combination and reject extreme words such as ‘entirely’, ‘exclusively’ and ‘without’.
135.sec: Universal angles

135.s:
With reference to India’s import duties on gold and silver in May 2026, consider the following statements:
1. The import duty was increased from 6 per cent to 15 per cent.
2. The increase resulted in a more than twofold rise in the duty rate.
3. Bullion imports became negligible after the increase.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
135.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the duty rose from 6 per cent to 15 per cent, which is more than double. Statement 3 is false because bullion imports remained robust.
135.tq: Check the numerical change first and reject the statement that reverses the stated trend.
135.sec: Universal angles

135.s: Which one of the following correctly describes Andhra Pradesh’s position in tobacco production and trade-related institutions?
o: It is among the top three tobacco-producing States and accounts for about 25 per cent of India’s output; the Tobacco Board is located in Guntur.
It produces only traditional Indian crops, while tobacco is an Old World crop administered from Hyderabad.
It is among the top five tobacco-producing States and accounts for about 10 per cent of India’s output; the Tobacco Board is located in Masulipatnam.
It is the sole tobacco-producing State in India and accounts for more than half of national output; the Tobacco Board is located in Machilipatnam.
135.x: Andhra Pradesh is among India’s top three tobacco producers and contributes about 25 per cent of national output. The Tobacco Board is situated in Guntur, and tobacco is a New World crop.
135.tq: Combine the ranking, percentage, location and crop-origin clues while rejecting exaggerated figures and reversed facts.
135.sec: Universal angles

135.s: What was one important economic consequence of collecting land revenue in cash under the zabt system?
o: It monetised the rural economy and linked peasants to markets.
It replaced agricultural production with pastoral activity.
It abolished all forms of rural credit.
It weakened the connection between peasants and markets.
135.x: Cash revenue under zabt monetised the rural economy and connected peasants with markets. The system did not abolish rural credit or replace agriculture with pastoralism.
135.tq: Apply the cause-and-effect relationship to the economic role of cash revenue.
135.sec: Universal angles

135.s: Masulipatnam was important in the Qutb Shahi period primarily because it served as the
o: first European trade centre established by the Dutch in Andhra
Qutb Shahi gateway for overseas commerce
principal Mughal mint for copper coins
135.x: Masulipatnam functioned as the Qutb Shahi gateway for overseas commerce. The Tobacco Board was located in Guntur, while the first European trade centre in Andhra was established at Machilipatnam.
135.tq: Use location-based discrimination among closely related Andhra commercial centres.
135.sec: Universal angles

135.s:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
A. Dutch establishment of a European trade centre at Machilipatnam
B. Grant of Bangaru Farmana by Abdullah Qutb Shah to the English
C. Increase of India’s import duty on gold and silver from 6 per cent to 15 per cent
135.x: The Dutch established the trade centre at Machilipatnam in 1605, Bangaru Farmana was issued in 1636, and the import-duty increase occurred in May 2026.
135.tq: Place the two seventeenth-century events before the modern event, then distinguish 1605 from 1636.
135.sec: Universal angles

135.s: The first European trade centre in Andhra during the early modern period was established at
o: Masulipatnam as a Qutb Shahi administrative capital
135.x: Machilipatnam was the first European trade centre in Andhra, established by the Dutch in 1605. Guntur was associated with the Tobacco Board, while Masulipatnam is identified as the Qutb Shahi gateway.
135.tq: Distinguish the closely related names and match the place with its specific commercial role.
135.sec: Universal angles

135.s: Bangaru Farmana, issued in 1636, is associated with which of the following?
o: The establishment of the Tobacco Board at Guntur
The Dutch establishment of the first European trade centre in Andhra
Abdullah Qutb Shah’s grant of trade concessions to the English
The Mughal introduction of the zabt revenue system
135.x: Abdullah Qutb Shah issued the Bangaru Farmana in 1636, granting trade concessions to the English. The Dutch trade centre at Machilipatnam dates to 1605, whereas zabt and the Tobacco Board relate to different contexts.
135.tq: Match the named document with its issuer, date and beneficiaries; swapped authorities are the main trap.
135.sec: Universal angles

135.s:
Consider the following statements regarding François Bernier’s view of land ownership in Mughal India:
1. Bernier expressed the view that there was no private property in land.
2. This view is accepted without qualification by all modern historians.
3. Modern historians have contested Bernier’s interpretation.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
135.x: Bernier did express the view that private property in land did not exist. However, modern historians have contested this interpretation, so statement 2 is false and statement 3 is correct.
135.tq: Find the qualified historical interpretation and reject the absolute claim ‘all modern historians’.
135.sec: Universal angles

135.s:
Assertion (A): Cash revenue under the Mughal zabt system helped link peasants with markets.
Reason (R): The collection of revenue in cash contributed to the monetisation of the rural economy.

Choose the correct answer.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
135.x: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true. Cash collection monetised rural economic activity, thereby connecting peasants more closely with markets.
135.tq: Test whether the stated economic consequence follows directly from the mechanism given in the Reason.
135.sec: Universal angles

136.s: Francois Bernier, who visited the Mughal Empire during 1656–1668, was associated with which of the following positions and patrons?
o: Physician of Shah Jahan and patronised by Mir Jumla
Physician of Dara Shikoh and patronised by Danishmand Khan
Physician of Aurangzeb and patronised by Shaista Khan
Physician of Jahangir and patronised by Asaf Khan
136.x: Francois Bernier was a French doctor who served as physician to Dara Shikoh and received the patronage of Danishmand Khan.
136.tq: Match the foreign traveller with his precise post and patron.

136.s: Who among the following wrote Travels in the Mogul Empire?
136.x: Francois Bernier wrote Travels in the Mogul Empire, an important account of Mughal society during 1656–1668.

136.s: Which one of the following observations is associated with Francois Bernier?
o: He described only the diamond mines of the Deccan.
He wrote exclusively about the famine during Shah Jahan’s reign.
He observed six cases of sati and commented on superstition across religions.
He recorded 20,000 registered prostitutes in Hyderabad.
136.x: Bernier recorded six cases of sati and commented on superstition among different religious communities.
136.tq: Use the traveller–observation association rather than the traveller’s nationality alone.
136.sec: Foreign travellers - account of Mughal society and post held  [other exams]

136.x: J.B. Tavernier was a French gem merchant who visited the courts of Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb six times.

136.s: Which of the following was written by J.B. Tavernier?
o: A New Account of East India and Persia
136.x: Tavernier wrote Six Voyages and described diamond mines, the Peacock Throne and sati.
136.tq: Author–work discrimination among closely related travel accounts.
136.sec: Foreign travellers - account of Mughal society and post held  [other exams]

136.s:
Consider the following statements about Niccolao Manucci:
