182.x: P.E. Roberts was associated with the description of the revolt as “just a sepoy mutiny,” not with a work titled *The Causes of the Indian Revolt*. *Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind*, meaning “The Causes of the Indian Revolt,” was written by Sir Syed Ahmed Khan.
182.tq: Detect the familiar title wrongly assigned to a different author.
182.sec: Contemporary Indian writings on the causes - author and book

182.s: P.E. Roberts described the Revolt of 1857 as:
o: A religious war against the British
The First War of Indian Independence
182.x: P.E. Roberts characterized the revolt as “just a sepoy mutiny,” particularly in connection with the cartridge issue.
182.tq: Separate the British interpretive label from the nationalist interpretation.
182.sec: Contemporary Indian writings on the causes - author and book

182.s:
According to Sir Syed Ahmed Khan, which of the following contributed to the outbreak of the Revolt of 1857?
1. Lack of Indian representation in the Legislative Council
2. Misunderstanding of Indian customs
3. Complete equality between Indian and British soldiers
Which of the statements given above are correct?
182.x: Sir Syed Ahmed Khan blamed the lack of Indian representation in the Legislative Council and the misunderstanding of Indian customs. Complete equality between Indian and British soldiers was not a cause identified by him.
182.tq: Use the contradiction in the third statement to isolate the two supported causes.
182.sec: Contemporary Indian writings on the causes - author and book

182.s: Which one of the following mutinies took place in July 1806?
o: Barrackpore mutiny of the 34th Native Infantry
Barrackpore mutiny of the 47th Native Infantry
182.x: The Vellore mutiny took place in July 1806. It was associated with the controversial military dress regulations and religious apprehensions.
182.tq: Use the direct date–event association.
182.sec: Earlier sepoy mutinies - causes and dates  [other exams]

182.s: The Vellore mutiny of 1806 was chiefly triggered by which of the following measures?
o: Introduction of a new dress code and prohibition of caste marks and earrings
Refusal to cross the sea to Burma
Refusal to use the new rifle cartridges
182.x: The new dress code, including a turban with a leather cockade and restrictions on caste marks and earrings, caused resentment among the sepoys at Vellore.
182.tq: Distinguish the cause attached to a specific mutiny.
182.sec: Earlier sepoy mutinies - causes and dates  [other exams]

182.s: The Barrackpore mutiny of November 1824 was caused by the sepoys’ refusal to—
182.x: The 47th Native Infantry at Barrackpore refused to go to Burma by sea during the First Anglo-Burmese War.
182.tq: Apply the who–cause–event linkage.
182.sec: Earlier sepoy mutinies - causes and dates  [other exams]

182.s:
Consider the following pairs:
a. Vellore mutiny — July 1806
b. Barrackpore mutiny of the 47th Native Infantry — November 1824
c. Berhampur mutiny of the 19th Native Infantry — February 1857
d. Barrackpore mutiny of the 34th Native Infantry — 29 March 1857
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
182.x: All four pairs are correctly matched. Berhampur involved refusal of the new cartridges, while Mangal Pandey’s attack at Barrackpore occurred on 29 March 1857.
182.tq: Start from the sure date–event pairs and eliminate mismatched combinations.
182.sec: Earlier sepoy mutinies - causes and dates  [other exams]

182.s: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: 38th Native Infantry — Refusal to go to Burma in 1852
19th Native Infantry — Attack on officers at Barrackpore on 29 March 1857
182.x: The attack at Barrackpore on 29 March 1857 was carried out by Mangal Pandey of the 34th Native Infantry. The 19th Native Infantry at Berhampur refused the new cartridges in February 1857.
182.tq: Find the wrong person–regiment association.
182.sec: Earlier sepoy mutinies - causes and dates  [other exams]

182.s: The Santhal revolt of 1855–56 is distinguished from the mutinies listed in the context of the 1857 uprising because it was—
o: the first mutiny of the 34th Native Infantry
a civil revolt rather than a sepoy revolt
an uprising caused by the new cartridges
a military revolt over sea service
182.x: The Santhal revolt of 1855–56 was a civil revolt and not a sepoy mutiny.
182.tq: Separate a civil revolt from a military mutiny.
182.sec: Earlier sepoy mutinies - causes and dates  [other exams]

182.s:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
A. Barrackpore mutiny of the 47th Native Infantry
B. Vellore mutiny
C. Berhampur refusal of the new cartridges
D. Mangal Pandey’s attack at Barrackpore
182.x: The correct sequence is Vellore mutiny in July 1806, Barrackpore mutiny in November 1824, Berhampur in February 1857 and Mangal Pandey’s attack on 29 March 1857.
182.tq: Fix the earliest and latest events first, then place the intervening events.
182.sec: Earlier sepoy mutinies - causes and dates  [other exams]

182.s: Mangal Pandey was hanged and his regiment was disbanded on—
182.x: Mangal Pandey was hanged and the regiment was disbanded on 8 April 1857. His attack had taken place earlier, on 29 March 1857.
182.tq: Distinguish closely spaced dates in a sequence of events.
182.sec: Earlier sepoy mutinies - causes and dates  [other exams]

182.s: What immediately preceded the Meerut rising of 10 May 1857?
o: The proclamation of Bahadur Shah II as Shahenshah-e-Hindustan
The sentencing of 85 sepoys of the 3rd Native Cavalry to ten years’ imprisonment
The disbandment of Mangal Pandey’s regiment
The refusal of the 19th Native Infantry to use the rifle
182.x: On 9 May 1857, 85 sepoys of the 3rd Native Cavalry at Meerut were sentenced to ten years. The rising followed on 10 May, when officers were shot and imprisoned comrades were freed.
182.tq: Identify the immediately preceding event rather than the later consequence.
182.sec: Earlier sepoy mutinies - causes and dates  [other exams]

182.s: The rebels who reached Delhi on 11–12 May 1857 proclaimed whom as Shahenshah-e-Hindustan?
182.x: After reaching Delhi, the rebels proclaimed Bahadur Shah II as Shahenshah-e-Hindustan on 11–12 May 1857.
182.tq: Match the political title with the associated leader.
182.sec: Earlier sepoy mutinies - causes and dates  [other exams]

182.s: The abolition of Sati in 1829 was resented by orthodox sections primarily because it was viewed as—
o: an attempt to abolish temple taxation
182.x: The abolition of Sati was perceived by orthodox groups as interference in established custom.
182.tq: Link a social law with the specific form of resentment it generated.
182.sec: Socio-religious causes - social laws, missionaries  [other exams]

182.s: Which British Governor-General is associated with the abolition of Sati in 1829?
182.x: The abolition of Sati in 1829 was carried out during the tenure of Lord William Bentinck.
182.tq: Use the reformer–reform association while avoiding ruler-swapping traps.
182.sec: Socio-religious causes - social laws, missionaries  [other exams]

182.s: The Lex Loci Act, also known as the Religious or Caste Disabilities Act, was enacted in—
182.x: The Religious Disabilities Act, also called the Caste Disabilities Removal Act or Lex Loci Act, was enacted in 1850.
182.tq: Discriminate between closely related reform dates.
182.sec: Socio-religious causes - social laws, missionaries  [other exams]

182.s: What provision of the Religious Disabilities Act of 1850 particularly alarmed orthodox sections?
o: It prohibited the taxation of religious lands
It abolished the zamindari system throughout India
It permitted converts to Christianity to inherit ancestral property
It granted sepoys exemption from overseas service
182.x: The Act enabled converts to Christianity to inherit ancestral property, which was viewed as an incentive for conversion.
182.tq: Identify the practical consequence behind a source of religious apprehension.
182.sec: Socio-religious causes - social laws, missionaries  [other exams]

182.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Christian missionaries preached under police protection.
2. Missionaries criticised Hindu and Islamic practices.
3. Western education, railways and the telegraph generated fears of mass conversion.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
182.x: All three statements are correct. Missionary activity under official protection and the spread of Western institutions created apprehensions about religious conversion and the loss of caste identity.
182.tq: Test a cluster of related causes through an all-inclusive option.
182.sec: Socio-religious causes - social laws, missionaries  [other exams]

182.s: Which of the following was NOT among the socio-religious apprehensions that contributed to discontent before 1857?
o: Complete withdrawal of missionary activity from British India
Social discrimination and racial arrogance of officials
Taxation of temple and mosque lands
Laws against child marriage and female infanticide
182.x: Missionaries operated under police protection; their activity was not completely withdrawn. Taxation of religious lands, social legislation, racial arrogance and discrimination contributed to resentment.
182.tq: Reject the absolute reversal of a stated condition.
182.sec: Socio-religious causes - social laws, missionaries  [other exams]

182.s: Under the Permanent, Ryotwari and Mahalwari systems, the principal economic burden on peasants was—
o: rigid collection of high land revenue
182.x: High land revenue was collected rigidly under the Permanent, Ryotwari and Mahalwari settlements, placing severe pressure on peasants.
182.tq: Identify the common feature shared by different revenue settlements.
182.sec: Economic causes - revenue settlements, taluqdars, Inam Commission, artisans

182.s: What was a major consequence of the high and rigid land revenue demand on peasants?
o: They became independent of moneylenders and traders
They were driven into debt and lost land to moneylenders and traders
They were exempted from commercial cultivation
182.x: The heavy revenue burden pushed peasants into debt, often resulting in the loss of their land to moneylenders and traders.
182.tq: Follow the economic cause to its immediate social consequence.
182.sec: Economic causes - revenue settlements, taluqdars, Inam Commission, artisans

182.s: Commercialisation of agriculture under British rule often compelled peasants to—
o: cultivate cash crops under high taxation
produce goods exclusively for princely courts
grow only food grains for local consumption
182.x: Commercialisation forced peasants to grow cash crops while they continued to face high land revenue demands.
182.tq: Apply the definition of commercialisation to the agrarian situation.
182.sec: Economic causes - revenue settlements, taluqdars, Inam Commission, artisans

182.s: The taluqdars of Awadh lost their estates under the—
182.x: The taluqdars of Awadh lost their estates under the summary settlement of 1856, making them strongly anti-British.
182.tq: Match the affected landed group with the correct administrative measure and year.
182.sec: Economic causes - revenue settlements, taluqdars, Inam Commission, artisans

182.s: The Inam Commission, established in Bombay in 1852, is associated with the confiscation of approximately—
182.x: The Inam Commission confiscated about 20,000 estates whose owners could not produce valid title deeds.
182.tq: Use the distinctive quantitative figure attached to an institution.
182.sec: Economic causes - revenue settlements, taluqdars, Inam Commission, artisans

182.s: Why did the actions of the Inam Commission create resentment among landholders?
o: It transferred all estates to Indian artisans
It confiscated estates when owners could not show title
It abolished all taxation on religious lands
It restored estates without examining ownership claims
182.x: The Commission confiscated estates whose owners were unable to establish legal title, thereby creating insecurity among landholders.
182.tq: Connect an institution’s procedure with its political consequence.
182.sec: Economic causes - revenue settlements, taluqdars, Inam Commission, artisans

182.s: Which of the following best explains the ruin of Indian artisans and handicrafts before 1857?
o: The Industrial Revolution reduced the supply of British textiles
Indian handicrafts received increased princely patronage after annexations
British machine-made goods entered duty-free, while Indian goods faced heavy tariffs
British goods were excluded from Indian markets
182.x: Cheap British machine-made goods entered India with favourable treatment, while Indian goods faced heavy tariffs, contributing to deindustrialisation.
182.tq: Compare unequal trade treatment rather than focusing on only one factor.
182.sec: Economic causes - revenue settlements, taluqdars, Inam Commission, artisans

182.s:
The decline of traditional artisans was aggravated by which combination of factors?
1. Cheap British machine-made goods, especially textiles
2. Loss of princely court patronage after annexations
3. Increased demand for indigenous handicrafts by annexed courts
Which of the statements given above are correct?
182.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Annexations ended princely patronage, while British machine-made goods, particularly textiles, damaged Indian handicrafts; statement 3 reverses this effect.
182.tq: Find the statement that reverses the stated economic trend.
182.sec: Economic causes - revenue settlements, taluqdars, Inam Commission, artisans

182.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Indian artisans — Deindustrialisation due to machine-made imports
Taluqdars of Awadh — Loss of estates under the 1856 summary settlement
Absentee sovereignty — Expansion of princely court patronage
182.x: Absentee sovereignty was associated with the drain of wealth to Britain, not with the expansion of princely court patronage. The other three pairs are correctly matched.
182.tq: Detect the reversed economic relationship in the final pair.
182.sec: Economic causes - revenue settlements, taluqdars, Inam Commission, artisans

182.s: The terms ‘absentee sovereignty’ and ‘drain of wealth’ in the context of the causes of 1857 refer primarily to—
o: the movement of peasants from villages to princely courts
the transfer of religious authority from temples to courts
the transfer of economic resources from India to Britain
the migration of British officials to Indian villages
182.x: Absentee sovereignty involved the extraction and transfer of wealth from India to Britain, contributing to economic resentment.
182.tq: Distinguish an economic concept from unrelated administrative or religious processes.
182.sec: Economic causes - revenue settlements, taluqdars, Inam Commission, artisans

182.s: Which of the following was an administrative cause of resentment before the Revolt of 1857?
o: Exclusion of Indians from high civil and military posts
Rapid and inexpensive justice for all social groups
Abolition of corruption in lower courts
Admission of Indians to all high civil and military posts
182.x: Indians were excluded from high civil and military posts, producing resentment against the colonial administrative structure.
182.tq: Identify the discriminatory administrative practice.
182.sec: Administrative causes - exclusion from high posts, corrupt courts and police

182.s:
Consider the following statements about the lower courts and police before 1857:
1. Corruption was rampant.
2. Justice was slow and costly.
3. The system generally favoured the poor over the rich.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
182.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The judicial system was slow, costly and generally favoured the rich, making statement 3 incorrect.
182.tq: Use the reversed comparison trap in the third statement.
182.sec: Administrative causes - exclusion from high posts, corrupt courts and police

182.s: The annexation of princely states adversely affected the colonial administration because it—
o: ended the drain of wealth to Britain
created employment for thousands of court officials and soldiers
restored the authority of all displaced rulers
threw officials, retainers and soldiers of princely courts out of work
182.x: Annexations displaced thousands of officials, retainers and soldiers who had depended on princely courts for employment and patronage.
182.tq: Trace the administrative consequence of annexation.
182.sec: Administrative causes - exclusion from high posts, corrupt courts and police

182.s: Which one of the following most accurately describes the character of British administration that contributed to discontent before 1857?
o: Administration based on complete equality in high posts
Inefficient and prejudiced administration with corruption in police and lower courts
Administration controlled entirely by Indian officials
182.x: The administration was inefficient and prejudiced; corruption was widespread in the police and lower courts, while Indians were excluded from high posts.
182.tq: Select the precise composite description rather than an absolute claim.
182.sec: Administrative causes - exclusion from high posts, corrupt courts and police

182.s:
Which of the following territories were annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse before the Revolt of 1857?
1. Satara
2. Jhansi
3. Nagpur
4. Awadh
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
182.x: Satara, Jhansi and Nagpur were annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse. Awadh was annexed separately in 1856 on the ground of misgovernance.
182.tq: Separate the territories taken under the Doctrine of Lapse from Awadh, which was annexed on a different ground.
182.sec: Political causes - Doctrine of Lapse, Awadh, the Mughal emperor

182.s: Rani Lakshmibai became hostile to the British primarily because
o: her pension was stopped after the annexation of Awadh
she was prevented from retaining her estates under the Summary Settlement
her adopted son was refused the throne of Jhansi
the Mughal emperor withdrew recognition of her kingdom
182.x: The adopted son of Rani Lakshmibai was refused succession to the throne of Jhansi under the Doctrine of Lapse.
182.tq: Match the ruler with the specific grievance attributed to her.
182.sec: Political causes - Doctrine of Lapse, Awadh, the Mughal emperor

182.s: Nana Saheb was discontented with the British because he was
o: deprived of his estate under the Summary Settlement of Awadh
refused the title of Mughal emperor
not allowed to retain his fort at Jhansi
182.x: Nana Saheb was denied the pension that had been enjoyed by his predecessor, creating a major political grievance against the British.
182.tq: Use the person–grievance pairing rather than confusing Nana Saheb with the rulers of Jhansi or Awadh.
182.sec: Political causes - Doctrine of Lapse, Awadh, the Mughal emperor

182.s: Awadh was annexed by the British in 1856 on the alleged ground of
o: failure to pay tribute to the Mughal emperor
182.x: Awadh was annexed in 1856 on the ground of alleged misgovernance. It was not annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse.
182.tq: Distinguish the stated ground for Awadh’s annexation from the Doctrine of Lapse.
182.sec: Political causes - Doctrine of Lapse, Awadh, the Mughal emperor

182.s:
The annexation of Awadh adversely affected which of the following groups by depriving them of their livelihoods?
1. Lords
2. Officials
3. Retainers
4. Soldiers
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
182.x: The annexation of Awadh deprived lords, officials, retainers and soldiers of their livelihoods. All four groups were affected by the political change.
182.tq: Check whether the complete list of groups affected by annexation has been retained.
182.sec: Political causes - Doctrine of Lapse, Awadh, the Mughal emperor

182.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the taluqdars of Awadh:
1. About 21,000 taluqdars were dispossessed of their estates.
2. Their estates were affected under the Summary Settlement of 1856.
3. They were allowed to retain all their arms and forts.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
182.x: About 21,000 taluqdars were dispossessed of their estates under the Summary Settlement of 1856. They were not allowed to retain their arms and forts, so statement 3 is false.
182.tq: Spot the reversed statement about the restrictions imposed on the taluqdars.
182.sec: Political causes - Doctrine of Lapse, Awadh, the Mughal emperor

182.s: Which one of the following statements regarding Bahadur Shah Zafar is correct?
o: He was deposed in 1856 after the annexation of Awadh.
He was informed that his successors would lose the Red Fort and the royal title.
He was prevented from retaining arms and forts in Awadh.
He was denied a pension because of the Doctrine of Lapse.
182.x: Bahadur Shah Zafar was told that his successors would lose the Red Fort, and Canning announced that they would also lose the royal title.
182.tq: Keep the Mughal emperor’s threatened succession rights distinct from the grievances of Awadh and Jhansi.
182.sec: Political causes - Doctrine of Lapse, Awadh, the Mughal emperor

182.s: Who announced that the successors of Bahadur Shah Zafar would lose the royal title?
182.x: Canning announced that the successors of Bahadur Shah Zafar would lose the royal title, in addition to being removed from the Red Fort.
182.tq: Use the authority–decision association and avoid swapping British officials with Indian rulers.
182.sec: Political causes - Doctrine of Lapse, Awadh, the Mughal emperor

182.s:
Which of the following developments contributed to the perception of British rule as ‘absentee sovereignty’?
1. Disbanding of the Pindaris
2. Disbanding of irregular soldiers
3. Withdrawal of the Mughal royal title immediately after the annexation of Awadh
4. Displacement of established political and military interests
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
182.x: The disbanding of the Pindaris and irregular soldiers, along with the displacement of established political and military interests, contributed to the perception of absentee sovereignty. The withdrawal of the Mughal royal title was a separate threatened measure.
182.tq: Reject the statement that combines a related but temporally distinct Mughal measure with the causes of absentee sovereignty.
182.sec: Political causes - Doctrine of Lapse, Awadh, the Mughal emperor

182.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Roberts — Revolt as the first war of independence
Savarkar — Revolt as a sepoy mutiny
Roberts — Revolt as a sepoy mutiny
Canning — Revolt as a peasant uprising only
182.x: Roberts described the event as a ‘sepoy mutiny’, whereas Savarkar described it as the ‘first war of independence’.
182.tq: Discriminate between similar historical interpretations by matching each label with its associated thinker.
182.sec: Universal angles

182.s: The Revolt of 1857 is described as combining the grievances of
o: rulers, peasants, soldiers and common people
urban merchants and British officials alone
missionaries, taluqdars and European soldiers only
182.x: The revolt brought together the grievances of rulers, peasants, soldiers and common people. It therefore had participation and causes extending beyond the sepoy ranks.
182.tq: Choose the complete social composition rather than the narrower sepoy-only interpretation.
182.sec: Universal angles

182.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Syed Ahmed Khan — first Indian-language work on the causes of the Revolt of 1857
Mangal Pandey — author of the first Indian-language work on the causes of the revolt
Savarkar — first martyr of the Revolt of 1857
Bahadur Shah Zafar — author of the first Indian-language work on the revolt
182.x: Syed Ahmed Khan is associated with the first Indian-language work on the causes of the Revolt of 1857.
182.tq: Match the ‘first’ distinction with the correct person and avoid confusing authorship with martyrdom.
182.sec: Universal angles

182.s: Who is regarded as the first martyr of the Revolt of 1857?
182.x: Mangal Pandey is identified as the first martyr of the Revolt of 1857.
182.tq: Test a first-in-sequence fact directly, while using other prominent figures as nearby distractors.
182.sec: Universal angles

182.s:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
A. Introduction of the Enfield rifle
B. Annexation of Awadh
C. Barrackpore attack by Mangal Pandey
D. Promise of religious neutrality by the Crown
182.x: The Enfield rifle was introduced in 1853, Awadh was annexed in 1856, Mangal Pandey attacked at Barrackpore on 29 March 1857, and the Crown’s promise of religious neutrality followed after 1858.
182.tq: Fix the dated anchors first and then place the post-1857 Crown policy last.
182.sec: Universal angles

182.s:
With reference to the post-1857 policy of the British Crown, consider the following statements:
1. The Crown promised religious neutrality.
2. State patronage of missionary work was withdrawn.
3. The policy formally expanded state support for missionary activities.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
182.x: After 1858, the Crown promised religious neutrality and withdrew state patronage from missionary work. Statement 3 reverses this policy.
182.tq: Identify the reversed policy statement in a post-revolt administrative change.
182.sec: Universal angles

182.s: On 21 July 2026, the Prime Minister paid tribute to Mangal Pandey in connection with his
182.x: The Prime Minister paid tribute to Mangal Pandey on 21 July 2026 on the occasion of his birth anniversary. Mangal Pandey was born on 19 July 1827.
182.tq: Separate the date of the tribute from the date of birth and from the events of March 1857.
182.sec: Universal angles

182.s:
Which of the following statements regarding Mangal Pandey is correct?
1. He was born on 19 July 1827.
2. He attacked Lieutenant Baugh and Sergeant-Major Hewson at Barrackpore on 29 March 1857.
3. The incident was associated with the 1853 Enfield rifle.
4. He was subsequently hanged.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
182.x: Mangal Pandey was born on 19 July 1827, attacked Lieutenant Baugh and Sergeant-Major Hewson at Barrackpore on 29 March 1857 in the context of the Enfield rifle controversy, and was subsequently hanged.
182.tq: Retain all four linked biographical and event details instead of selecting only the Barrackpore incident.
182.sec: Universal angles

183.s: Who led the defence of Delhi during the Revolt of 1857 as the real military leader, while Bahadur Shah Zafar remained the nominal leader?
183.x: General Bakht Khan was the real military leader at Delhi, whereas Bahadur Shah Zafar was the nominal leader.
183.tq: Distinguish the nominal authority from the actual military commander.

183.s: General Bakht Khan led which body at Delhi during the Revolt of 1857?
183.x: Bakht Khan led a 10-member Court of Soldiers at Delhi.
183.tq: Use the distinctive numerical composition to identify the correct institution.

183.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
183.x: Khan Bahadur Khan led the revolt at Bareilly. Maulvi Ahmadullah was associated with Faizabad, Maulvi Liyakat Ali with Allahabad and Banaras, and Shah Mal with Baraut.
183.tq: Eliminate options by checking the leader against the centre of operation.

183.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the revolt at Lucknow:
1. Begum Hazrat Mahal led the revolt.
2. She declared her son Birjis Qadr the ruler of Awadh.
3. Hindus and Muslims shared offices under the arrangement established there.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
183.x: All three statements are correct. Begum Hazrat Mahal led at Lucknow, proclaimed Birjis Qadr ruler of Awadh, and the administration included both Hindus and Muslims in offices.
183.tq: Check whether all details associated with one centre are simultaneously correct.

183.s: Rani Lakshmibai was proclaimed head of state at Jhansi on:
183.x: Rani Lakshmibai was proclaimed head of state at Jhansi on 4 June 1858.
183.tq: Separate closely related dates connected with the same leader.

183.s: Which of the following statements about the revolt at Gwalior is correct?
o: It was captured by Kunwar Singh and Nana Saheb.
It was led exclusively by Bahadur Shah Zafar.
It remained under Scindia throughout the revolt.
It was captured by Lakshmibai and Tantia Tope, after which Scindia fled to Agra.
183.x: Rani Lakshmibai and Tantia Tope captured Gwalior, while Scindia fled to Agra.
183.tq: Use the leader–event–consequence chain to reject swapped associations.

183.s: The revolt at Bareilly was led by Khan Bahadur Khan, who proclaimed himself:
183.x: Khan Bahadur Khan proclaimed himself Nawab Nizam at Bareilly and commanded an army of about 40,000.
183.tq: Test the exact title adopted by a regional leader.

183.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Allahabad and Banaras — Khan Bahadur Khan
183.x: Allahabad and Banaras were associated with Maulvi Liyakat Ali, not Khan Bahadur Khan. Khan Bahadur Khan led at Bareilly.
183.tq: Find the swapped leader–centre pair.

183.s: Shah Mal mobilised the headmen and cultivators of which area during the Revolt of 1857?
o: The chaurasee des of 84 villages in Baraut
183.x: Shah Mal mobilised the chaurasee des, meaning the area of 84 villages, in the Baraut region of Uttar Pradesh.
183.tq: Identify the distinctive local organisation and its numerical extent.

183.s:
Which of the following leaders and areas of operation is correctly matched?
1. Khan Bahadur Khan — Rohilkhand
2. Maulvi Ahmadullah — Faizabad
3. Kunwar Singh — Bihar
4. Tantia Tope — Central India
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
183.x: All four pairs are correct. Khan Bahadur Khan operated in Rohilkhand, Ahmadullah in Faizabad, Kunwar Singh in Bihar, and Tantia Tope continued guerrilla warfare in Central India.
183.tq: Verify each leader–region pair before selecting the coded combination.

183.s: Who betrayed Tantia Tope, leading to his capture and execution?
183.x: Tantia Tope was betrayed by Man Singh, after which he was captured and executed.
183.tq: Distinguish the betrayer from other figures associated with the revolt.

183.s: Tantia Tope continued guerrilla warfare after Nana Saheb had:
183.x: Nana Saheb escaped to Nepal, while Tantia Tope continued guerrilla warfare in Central India.
183.tq: Separate the different fates of closely associated leaders.

183.s: Which one of the following leaders of the Revolt of 1857 was exiled to Rangoon?
183.x: Bahadur Shah Zafar was exiled to Rangoon after the suppression of the revolt.
183.tq: Match the leader with the eventual fate rather than the area of operation.

183.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Begum Hazrat Mahal escaped to Nepal.
2. Kunwar Singh died at Jagdishpur after being wounded.
3. Rani Lakshmibai died fighting at Gwalior.

Consider the following statements regarding the failure of the revolt of 1857:
1. It lacked an all-India character.
2. It had no unified ideology or forward-looking nationalist programme.
3. The rebels possessed superior arms and a centralised system of communication.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
184.x: The revolt lacked an all-India character and a unified modern nationalist programme. Statement 3 is false because the rebels had inferior arms and poor communication and coordination.
184.tq: Spot the reversed military and communication comparison.
184.sec: Reasons for failure - leadership, unity, plan, arms, communication, British strength

184.s: The military disadvantage of the rebels during the revolt was mainly due to their dependence on:
184.x: The rebels generally used swords, spears and old muskets, whereas the British had Enfield rifles and the electric telegraph.
184.tq: Compare the weaponry and communication systems of the two sides.
184.sec: Reasons for failure - leadership, unity, plan, arms, communication, British strength

184.s: Which one of the following was NOT a reason for the failure of the revolt of 1857?
o: Unified leadership under a modern nationalist programme
British ability to send troops from eastern, western and southern India
184.x: The revolt had no unified leadership or modern nationalist programme. The other options were factors contributing to its failure.
184.tq: Find the option that states the opposite of a recognised weakness.
184.sec: Reasons for failure - leadership, unity, plan, arms, communication, British strength

184.s: The revolt of 1857 was chiefly a revolt of the:
184.x: The revolt was chiefly of the Bengal Army; the Madras and Bombay armies largely remained loyal, while a Gorkha regiment assisted Campbell.
184.tq: Distinguish the principal rebel army from the loyal presidency armies.
184.sec: Rulers' stand during the revolt and the presidency armies

184.s: Which one of the following rulers was regarded as most loyal to the British during the revolt, although his troops deserted to Rani Lakshmibai?
184.x: Scindia of Gwalior was regarded as most loyal to the British, but his troops deserted to Rani Lakshmibai.
184.tq: Separate the ruler's stand from the conduct of his troops.
184.sec: Rulers' stand during the revolt and the presidency armies

184.s:
Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
1. Holkar of Indore — Supported the British
2. Sikh chiefs of Patiala, Nabha and Jind — Actively helped the British
3. Nizam Afzal-ud-Daula and Diwan Salar Jung I — Kept the Deccan quiet
4. Bhonsle state of Nagpur — Joined the revolt under its ruling prince
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
184.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is false because Nagpur had already been annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse in 1854, leaving no ruler to join the revolt.
184.tq: Use a wrong-status and wrong-timeline trap in a coded statement set.
184.sec: Rulers' stand during the revolt and the presidency armies

184.s: The larger states of Hyderabad, Mysore and the Rajput states generally:
o: Stayed out and ignored Bahadur Shah's appeals
Joined Bahadur Shah's appeal and led the revolt
Transferred their armies to Nana Saheb
Were annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse
184.x: Hyderabad, Mysore and the Rajput states stayed out of the revolt and ignored Bahadur Shah's appeals.
184.tq: Test the collective stand of the larger princely states.
184.sec: Rulers' stand during the revolt and the presidency armies

184.s: The loyal princes were described as “breakwaters to the storm” by:
184.x: The phrase “breakwaters to the storm” is attributed to Lord Canning, although some accounts credit Lord Elgin.
184.tq: Discriminate between two authorities associated with a memorable phrase.
184.sec: Rulers' stand during the revolt and the presidency armies

184.s: The educated middle class generally remained neutral during the revolt because it viewed it as:
o: A movement led by urban merchants
184.x: The educated middle class generally saw the revolt as a backward-looking feudal reaction and therefore remained neutral.
184.tq: Link a social class with its stated interpretation of the revolt.
184.sec: Indian classes that stayed aloof or took part

184.s: Which of the following groups acted as “breakwaters” during the revolt in order to protect their class interests?
184.x: Big zamindars and moneylenders acted as “breakwaters” because they sought to protect their class interests.
184.tq: Match the social group with its distinctive political role.
184.sec: Indian classes that stayed aloof or took part

184.s: Which one of the following groups did NOT support the revolt of 1857?
184.x: Merchants and the urban elite generally did not support the revolt. Sepoys, peasants, artisans and dispossessed rulers took part in it.
184.tq: Find the social group that remained aloof among participating groups.
184.sec: Indian classes that stayed aloof or took part

184.s:
Arrange the following centres in the chronological order in which they were retaken by the British:
A. Delhi
B. Kanpur
C. Jhansi
D. Gwalior
184.x: Delhi was retaken in September 1857, Kanpur in December 1857, Jhansi in April 1858 and Gwalior in June 1858.
184.tq: Use the first and last dates, then arrange the middle events.
184.sec: Recapture - centres retaken and British officers who fell

184.s: Delhi was retaken by the British under the leadership of:
184.x: John Nicholson led the British recapture of Delhi in September 1857 and was killed in the assault.
184.tq: Match the recaptured centre with the British officer.
184.sec: Recapture - centres retaken and British officers who fell

184.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
184.x: Bihar was associated with Kunwar Singh and was recaptured by William Taylor. John Nicholson was associated with the recapture of Delhi.
184.tq: Find the swapped officer–centre pair.
184.sec: Recapture - centres retaken and British officers who fell

184.s: Lucknow was finally retaken by the British in March 1858 after the efforts of:
184.x: Lucknow was relieved by Havelock-Outram and Campbell and was retaken in March 1858.

184.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Sir Henry Lawrence died during the siege of Lucknow.
2. General Neill and Havelock were among the officers killed at Lucknow.
3. John Nicholson was killed at Lucknow.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
184.x: Sir Henry Lawrence, General Neill and Havelock were associated with deaths at Lucknow. Statement 3 is false because Nicholson fell during the assault on Delhi.
184.tq: Separate officers killed at Lucknow from the officer killed at Delhi.
184.sec: Recapture - centres retaken and British officers who fell

184.s: Allahabad and Banaras were associated with the rebellion led by ______ and were recaptured by ______.
184.x: Maulvi Liyakat Ali led the rebellion at Allahabad and Banaras, which were recaptured by Colonel Neill.
184.tq: Match the rebel leader and British officer to the correct centres.
184.sec: Recapture - centres retaken and British officers who fell

184.s: Who among the following was the Commander-in-Chief during the suppression of the revolt of 1857?
184.x: Sir Colin Campbell was the Commander-in-Chief during the suppression and later became known as Lord Clyde. He took over after General Anson died in 1857.
184.tq: Distinguish the civil head from the military commander.
184.sec: Viceroy and Commander-in-Chief during suppression

184.s: Lord Canning was Governor-General from 1856 to 1858 and became the first Viceroy from:
184.x: Lord Canning served as Governor-General from 1856 to 1858 and became the first Viceroy in 1858, serving until 1862.
184.tq: Test the constitutional transition from Governor-General to Viceroy.
184.sec: Viceroy and Commander-in-Chief during suppression

184.s: Which of the following statements correctly describes the repression after the suppression of the revolt?
o: Only rebel leaders were fined, while ordinary rebels were released.
Rebels were generally pardoned without trial.
The British avoided punitive measures in Delhi.
Thousands of rebels were publicly executed after mock trials.
184.x: The repression was harsh; thousands of rebels were publicly executed after mock trials, and British troops also committed atrocities.
184.tq: Identify the precise description of the punitive policy.
184.sec: Repression measures - executions, Delhi's aftermath

184.s: After the recapture of Delhi, which of the following occurred?
o: Bahadur Shah was restored and his sons were pardoned.
Bahadur Shah was tried and deported, while his sons were shot by Hodson.
The Mughal line was strengthened under Birjis Qadir.
Bahadur Shah escaped to Nepal with Nana Saheb.
184.x: After Delhi was recaptured, Bahadur Shah was tried and deported, and his sons were shot by Hodson. The Mughal line consequently ended.
184.tq: Use the aftermath sequence to reject reversal and substitution traps.
184.sec: Repression measures - executions, Delhi's aftermath

184.s: Which one of the following developments marked the end of the Mughal line after the recapture of Delhi?
o: The exile of Nana Saheb to Rangoon
The death of Kunwar Singh at Jagdishpur
The surrender of Scindia at Gwalior
The trial and deportation of Bahadur Shah and the shooting of his sons by Hodson
184.x: The Mughal line ended after Bahadur Shah was tried and deported and his sons were shot by Hodson.
184.tq: Connect the political consequence with the specific Delhi aftermath.
184.sec: Repression measures - executions, Delhi's aftermath

184.s: By which time had the Revolt of 1857 been suppressed, after continuing for more than a year?
184.x: The revolt was suppressed by mid-1858, after continuing for more than a year.
184.tq: Use the precise time marker and eliminate years outside the stated range.
184.sec: Universal angles

184.s: Which one of the following best describes the historical significance of the suppression of the Revolt of 1857?
o: It ended all resistance to British rule in India permanently.
It resulted in the immediate withdrawal of the British from India.
Although suppressed, it shook British rule in India to its foundations.
It strengthened British rule without causing any major impact.
184.x: The revolt was suppressed by mid-1858, but its impact was profound because it shook British rule in India to its foundations.
184.tq: Choose the precise consequence while rejecting extreme claims such as ‘all’ and ‘immediate’.
184.sec: Universal angles

184.s: Rani Avantibai Lodhi, remembered for her resistance during the Revolt of 1857, belonged to which place?
184.x: Rani Avantibai Lodhi was the ruler of Ramgarh in Madhya Pradesh. The Battle of Kheri was fought near Mandla, but Mandla was not her place of association stated here.
184.tq: Distinguish the person’s place of association from the nearby location of the battle.
184.sec: Universal angles

184.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Rani Avantibai Lodhi:
1. She defeated Charles Waddington’s force at the Battle of Kheri near Mandla.
2. She died fighting in 1858.
3. She was associated with Ramgarh in Madhya Pradesh.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
184.x: All three statements are correct. Rani Avantibai Lodhi of Ramgarh defeated Charles Waddington’s force at Kheri near Mandla and died fighting in 1858.
184.tq: Verify each statement independently, especially the person–place–event combination.
184.sec: Universal angles

184.s: Rani Avantibai Lodhi was remembered on her martyrdom day on which date in 2026?
184.x: Rani Avantibai Lodhi was remembered on her martyrdom day on 1 September 2026.
184.tq: Test the exact date rather than confusing it with another significant national or revolt-related date.
184.sec: Universal angles

184.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Hyderabad during the Revolt of 1857:
1. Nizam Afzal-ud-Daula remained loyal to the British.
2. Salar Jung I remained loyal to the British.
3. The attack on the Hyderabad Residency on 17 July 1857 was repulsed.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
184.x: All three statements are correct. Nizam Afzal-ud-Daula and Salar Jung I stayed loyal, and the Hyderabad Residency attack of 17 July 1857 was repulsed.
184.tq: Combine the loyalty and event statements, checking the date and outcome separately.

i. Stayed loyal during the Revolt of 1857
ii. Stayed loyal during the Revolt of 1857

185.s: Which of the following historians characterised the uprising of 1857 as a purely military outbreak or a mere sepoy mutiny?
185.x: Sir John Lawrence, along with J.R. Seeley and Charles Raikes, regarded the uprising primarily as a sepoy mutiny and denied it a popular or national character.
185.tq: Match the historian with the distinctive verdict.

185.s: Who described the Revolt of 1857 as a conflict between civilisation and barbarism?
185.x: T.R. Holmes described the revolt as a conflict between civilisation and barbarism.
185.tq: Use the exact phrase to identify the associated historian.

185.s: The interpretation of the Revolt of 1857 as a war of fanatic religionists against Christians is associated with:
185.x: L.E.R. Rees interpreted the revolt as a war of fanatic religionists against Christians.
185.tq: Discriminate between historians whose interpretations concern religion and mutiny.

185.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: T.R. Holmes — Conflict between civilisation and barbarism
Benjamin Disraeli — National rising, not a mere mutiny
S.N. Sen — War of fanatic religionists against Christians
185.x: The description of the revolt as a war of fanatic religionists against Christians was given by L.E.R. Rees. S.N. Sen stated that a fight for religion ended as a war of independence.
185.tq: Find the swapped historian and verdict.

185.s:
Consider the following statements regarding interpretations of the Revolt of 1857:
1. Benjamin Disraeli regarded it as a national rising rather than a mere mutiny.
2. Karl Marx regarded it as a national revolt.
3. V.D. Savarkar regarded it as a planned First War of Indian Independence.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
185.x: All three statements are correct. Disraeli, Marx and Savarkar rejected the narrow interpretation of the revolt as merely a sepoy mutiny, though Savarkar gave it the specific nationalist title.
185.tq: Check each historian against the precise nationalist interpretation.

185.s: The statement that the uprising essentially represented a feudal rising was made by:
185.x: Jawaharlal Nehru described the uprising as essentially a feudal rising in The Discovery of India.
185.tq: Use the author-and-verdict association rather than the broader nationalist label.

185.s: “What began as a fight for religion ended as a war of independence” was the assessment of:
185.x: S.N. Sen concluded that the revolt began as a fight for religion but ultimately developed into a war of independence.
185.tq: Identify the historian from the famous concluding formulation.

185.s: With reference to the assessment of Indian nationalism in the middle of the nineteenth century, which of the following is correct?
o: It was rejected as embryonic by both R.C. Majumdar and S.N. Sen.
It had already become fully developed and uniform throughout India.
It was regarded as being only embryonic by R.C. Majumdar and S.N. Sen.
It was confined exclusively to the British army.
185.x: R.C. Majumdar and S.N. Sen both regarded Indian nationalism in the mid-nineteenth century as still embryonic.
185.tq: Avoid the extreme wording in the distractors and select the qualified description.

185.s: Which one of the following books was written by R.C. Majumdar?
o: The Sepoy Mutiny and the Revolt of 1857
Civil Rebellion in the Indian Mutinies
185.x: R.C. Majumdar wrote The Sepoy Mutiny and the Revolt of 1857, published in 1957.
185.tq: Distinguish similar 1857 titles by their authors.

Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below.

185.s: Who authored The Indian Mutiny of 1857?
185.x: The Indian Mutiny of 1857 was written by G.B. Malleson.

185.x: Christopher Hibbert authored The Great Mutiny.

185.s: Which of the following correctly describes the relationship between S.N. Sen's and R.C. Majumdar's centenary histories?
o: Majumdar's work was Government-commissioned, whereas Sen wrote independently outside the centenary project.
Sen's work was Government-commissioned, whereas Majumdar wrote independently after parting with the official project.
Both were official Government of India volumes and reached the same conclusion about independence.
185.x: S.N. Sen's Eighteen Fifty-Seven was the Government of India-commissioned centenary history. R.C. Majumdar wrote his 1957 work independently after parting with the official project.
185.tq: Compare the commissioning status and institutional context of the two works.

185.s:
Consider the following statements about the centenary histories of 1857:
1. S.N. Sen's Eighteen Fifty-Seven was published in 1957.
2. R.C. Majumdar's The Sepoy Mutiny and the Revolt of 1857 was also published in 1957.
3. Sen's interpretation was that the revolt began as a religious struggle and ended as a war of independence.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
185.x: All three statements are correct. Both books appeared in 1957, while Sen gave the revolt an evolutionary interpretation from a religious fight to a war of independence.
185.tq: Verify the common year first, then distinguish the two historians' verdicts.
185.sec: Centenary histories - S.N. Sen and R.C. Majumdar

185.s: R.C. Majumdar's interpretation of the Revolt of 1857 differs from the nationalist interpretation attributed to him in some classifications because he specifically argued that it was:
o: the first, national and completely successful war of independence
only a conflict between civilisation and barbarism
neither first, nor national, nor a war of independence
185.x: R.C. Majumdar's own verdict was that the revolt was neither the first nor national nor a war of independence, despite some classifications placing him in a broader nationalist school.
185.tq: Resolve the apparent contradiction by separating a school classification from the historian's own verdict.
185.sec: Centenary histories - S.N. Sen and R.C. Majumdar

185.s: The term 'Sepoy Mutiny' or 'Indian Mutiny' was predominantly used by which school of historians?
185.x: British or imperialist historians commonly used the labels Sepoy Mutiny or Indian Mutiny and denied the revolt a national character.
185.tq: Associate the label with the historiographical school that used it.

185.s: Which one of the following labels was particularly associated with Indian nationalist interpretations of the uprising of 1857?
185.x: Indian nationalist historians commonly used the label Great Rebellion, while First War of Independence was especially associated with V.D. Savarkar.
185.tq: Distinguish a broad nationalist label from the specific Savarkar formulation.

185.s: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: V.D. Savarkar — First War of Independence
British or imperialist school — Sepoy Mutiny
Other names — Religious Fanaticism and Administrative Blunders
185.x: Revolt of 1857 and Indian Insurrection are listed as other names. Religious fanaticism and administrative blunders were explanations associated with the British or imperialist interpretation.
185.tq: Separate labels from explanatory causes in a school-wise classification.

185.s: The interpretation of the Revolt of 1857 as a feudal reaction primarily emphasises the role of:
o: dispossessed princes and taluqdars attempting to restore their lost positions
urban middle classes demanding representative government
European merchants opposing the East India Company
185.x: The feudal-reaction interpretation highlights dispossessed princes and taluqdars such as Nana Saheb, Lakshmibai and Begum Hazrat Mahal, who sought to recover lost positions.
185.tq: Apply the interpretation to the social groups and motives it highlights.

185.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the limitations of describing the Revolt of 1857 as the First War of Independence:
1. There was no common goal among all the participants.
2. Modern nationalism had not yet emerged.
3. The revolt was confined largely to North India.
4. Most of India remained neutral.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
185.x: All four statements are cited as limitations: the revolt lacked a common goal, modern nationalism was not yet developed, its main spread was in North India, and most of India remained neutral.
185.tq: Test the complete set of qualifications rather than selecting only the geographical limitation.

185.s: Which of the following groups was specifically identified as largely uninvolved in the Revolt of 1857?
185.x: The elite and urban classes were largely uninvolved, which is one reason historians question whether the revolt can be called a fully national movement.
185.tq: Identify the social group omitted from the main participation pattern.

185.s: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels' articles on the uprising were compiled under which title?
o: The Sepoy Mutiny and the Revolt of 1857
Civil Rebellion in the Indian Mutinies
The First Indian War of Independence 1857-1859
185.x: Karl Marx's and Friedrich Engels' articles were compiled as The First Indian War of Independence 1857-1859.
185.tq: Match the compilation title with the pair of writers associated with it.

185.s:
Arrange the following works in chronological order of publication:
A. The Indian War of Independence, 1857
B. The Sepoy Mutiny and the Revolt of 1857
C. Eighteen Fifty-Seven
D. The First Indian War of Independence 1857-1859
185.x: The Indian War of Independence, 1857 was published in 1909; the Marx-Engels compilation covers 1857-1859; and both Majumdar's and Sen's books were published in 1957. Thus the order is A, D, B, C.
185.tq: Fix the early 1909 work first and then place the 1957 centenary works.

185.s: In the British Parliament, Benjamin Disraeli characterised the uprising of 1857 primarily as which of the following?
o: A religious war confined to Awadh
A purely military mutiny without popular support
185.x: Disraeli questioned whether the event was merely a military mutiny or a national revolt, and viewed it as a national rising.
185.tq: Distinguish between closely related historiographical descriptions.

185.s: Which one of the following was identified by Sir Syed Ahmad Khan as the main cause of the revolt of 1857?
o: The decline of the textile industry in Bengal
The annexation of Punjab by the British
The introduction of the Subsidiary Alliance
The absence of Indians in the Legislative Council
185.x: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan argued that the absence of Indians in the Legislative Council caused the rulers to misunderstand the ruled.
185.tq: Test the precise cause attributed by an identified contemporary observer.
185.sec: ■ Contemporary views - Disraeli, Marx, Syed Ahmad Khan

185.s: The work *Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind*, published in 1859, mainly argued that the British administration failed because it—
o: misunderstood the Indian people due to the absence of Indians in the Legislative Council
excluded Indian rulers from the army
introduced a uniform system of taxation throughout India
185.x: The work attributed the revolt mainly to the absence of Indian representation in the Legislative Council, which led to misunderstanding between rulers and ruled.
185.tq: Apply an author’s argument to its stated administrative cause.
185.sec: ■ Contemporary views - Disraeli, Marx, Syed Ahmad Khan

185.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Eric Stokes's interpretation of the revolt of 1857:
1. He emphasised local and agrarian studies.
2. He viewed the revolt as a combination of several peasant and elite risings.
3. He treated it as a single centrally directed national movement.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
185.x: Eric Stokes emphasised local agrarian studies and interpreted the revolt as multiple peasant and elite risings, not as one centrally directed movement.
185.tq: Find the statement that reverses a historian’s interpretation.
185.sec: ■ Subaltern and peasant perspectives - Eric Stokes, Rudrangshu Mukherjee

185.s: Rudrangshu Mukherjee’s *Awadh in Revolt* primarily examines—
o: the military organisation of the Bombay Army
the role of the educated middle class in Bengal
the activities of Indian revolutionaries abroad
popular resistance by peasants and taluqdars in Awadh
185.x: *Awadh in Revolt* focuses on the popular resistance of peasants and taluqdars in Awadh.
185.tq: Match a historian’s work with its specific regional and social focus.
185.sec: ■ Subaltern and peasant perspectives - Eric Stokes, Rudrangshu Mukherjee

185.s: Which one of the following best describes the initial character and subsequent spread of the revolt of 1857?
o: It began as a peasant movement and remained confined to villages
It began as a constitutional agitation and became a princely movement
It began as a religious reform movement and became an urban strike
It began as a military mutiny and rapidly developed into a popular rebellion
185.x: The revolt began among soldiers but quickly drew in rulers, peasants, soldiers and common people, becoming a wider popular rebellion.
185.tq: Test the transformation of an event from its initial to its later character.

185.s:
Consider the following statements about the national character of the revolt of 1857:
1. The idea of a single Indian nation-state had not yet emerged.
2. It was a modern nationalist movement based on a common programme for a future society.
3. It was a traditional uprising in which different classes defended local, economic and religious interests against a common foreign enemy.
Which of the statements given above are correct?

o: It failed militarily but seriously shook British rule.
Its failure left British rule completely unaffected.
It succeeded in establishing a united Indian nation-state.
It resulted immediately in the withdrawal of the British from India.
185.x: Although the revolt failed, it shook British rule and later became a source of inspiration for Indian nationalism.
